title: 6 takeaways from Detroit Lions’ 19-15 win against Minnesota Vikings
summary: Coming off their first divisional win of the season, the Detroit Lions faced the undefeated Minnesota Vikings in another NFC North battle. The game was another nail-biter, and the Lions’ offense was too much for the Vikings to slow down. Minnesota’s offense continued to struggle as they could only find the end zone once, which […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 01: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions catches the ball against Byron Murphy #7 of the Minnesota Vikings during the second quarter at Ford Field on November 01, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Coming off their first divisional win of the season, the Detroit Lions faced the undefeated Minnesota Vikings in another NFC North battle. The game was another nail-biter, and the Lions’ offense was too much for the Vikings to slow down. Minnesota’s offense continued to struggle as they could only find the end zone once, which isn’t enough to stay undefeated in the NFL. Detroit held on and handed the Vikings their first loss of the season, winning 19-15. Here are my six takeaways from the Lions’ win against the Vikings. This was a Jahmyr Gibbs takeover It took a while to work out, but running back Jahmyr Gibbs took the game over when the Lions needed it most. Quarterback Jared Goff faced heavy blitzing, and when you can run the ball well, it forces the defense to ease up on that blitz. Gibbs’s only touchdown of the game was his best run of the season, and Goff even got out to block for him, helping Gibbs get six on the play. Jahmyr Gibbs races into the end zone to give the Lions the lead! MINvsDET on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/X42rZbve42 — NFL (@NFL) November 1, 2026 That play sparked Gibbs to take over the game, finishing with 153 yards on 23 carries—and two catches for 15 yards. In the fourth quarter, when Detroit needed to drain the clock and win, Gibbs ran for gains of 14, eight, and six. I wasn’t expecting Gibbs to have a monster game against the Vikings this week, but he did. Sione Vaki can’t be ignored either While Gibbs will get a lot of the attention, backup running back Sione Vaki deserves a lot of credit for this win, too. Vaki, offensively, hadn’t done much in his career prior to this game, but he could become the Lions’ backup running back for the future after his Week 8 performance: Vaki had 11 carries for 65 yards and a catch for five yards. It wasn’t just the results of Vaki’s runs, it was how he was getting them that stood out. Sometimes Vaki broke tackles and got more yards; other times, his speed made him look like he got shot out of a cannon. Vaki had himself a game too, and without someone to give Gibbs a break, this offense wouldn’t have been as explosive as it was today. Refs did everything to help Minnesota, but it wasn’t enough This was the worst-officiated game of the Lions’ season. The first taunting penalty with wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown was understandable, and it was a dumb play by him. The taunting on wide receiver Jameson Williams, though? Awful call. Who knew spinning the ball near a foot is way different than just spinning the football? I don’t think Williams planted the ball by the feet on purpose; he just put it down to celebrate, so now he has to make sure he’s not near anyone? We all sadly remember the phantom facemask, but now the Lions are being called for phantom false starts, as left tackle Penei Sewell was called for back-to-back false starts when he didn’t move a muscle. We also learned that uncatchable passes can now be eligible for defensive pass interference calls, as Detroit was called for defensive pass interference on a throw that was clearly uncatchable. This game was heavily influenced by the officiating, as it cost a touchdown and pushed the Lions out of field-goal range on their opening drive. It’s sad how officiating can change a game like that. If you give St. Brown that touchdown and don’t give Williams that penalty, Detroit wins this game 29-15, and it’s a lot less stressful. Injuries are piling up Just when the Lions were getting healthier with multiple players returning from injuries, those same players—and more—are back to dealing with new injuries. Starting center Cade Mays left the game with an ankle injury and didn’t return. Safety Brian Branch struck EDGE DJ Wonnum on a tackle, and both of their helmets collided. Both players would be ruled out of the game with a concussion. The biggest loss was linebacker Jack Campbell, who left the game with a neck injury. He was motionless on the field and had to be taken off the field on a stretcher. Campbell is a huge part of the defense, and his absence opens a big hole in a defense that has improved the past three games. Detroit is already down linebacker Devin White, and rookie linebacker Jimmy Rolder was injured on the same play Campbell went down. Cornerback D.J. Reed left the game in the fourth quarter with a hip injury and didn’t return. Running back and kick returner Jacob Saylors left the game with a neck injury and didn’t return, knocking another kick returner out for the Lions. The silver lining is that Branch and Mays have been out for five games, so the team has players with experience in their spots. Center Juice Scruggs was playing well before Mays returned, so the offensive line doesn’t really miss a step. Defensive back Keith Abney II played safety against the Arizona Cardinals and got playing time against the Packers the week before. This team was doing well with injuries entering Sunday, but suddenly the number of players injured is giving flashbacks to the past two seasons. Losing star players like Branch and Campbell would be a huge hit to a defense that looks a lot better than it did in September. Brad Holmes is going to have to make a move at the trade deadline Before this game, Lions fans have been vocal about Lions general manager Brad Holmes making a trade. With so many injuries on Sunday, the pressure is really on Holmes to make a move. The trade deadline is Tuesday, November 10th, so they still have another game to play before they need to make a trade. With the team going international that week, though, they might want to make a trade soon so that player could play as early as in that Germany game. The big question is where do you get help at? The EDGE spot has depth with rookie Derrick Moore, Tyler Lacy, and Ahmed Hassanein. Linebacker is down Devin White, and Rolders’ status is unknown. The team may have only three healthy options: Derrick Barnes, Trevor Nowaske, and Malcolm Rodriguez. At secondary, cornerback has been a position fans have clamored for, and depth wouldn’t hurt. In the secondary, Lions head coach Dan Campbell said safety Thomas Harper could return soon, and Kerby Joseph started his 21-day window to see if he can get off PUP. Detroit could use help at many spots on defense, so maybe Holmes makes multiple trades. Either way, time is ticking away, and if you don’t want to lose the momentum you have right now, you have to make a move to help this team. Youth movement inbound The Lions have aimed to get younger overall, and the youth movement got a big push on Sunday. While it wasn’t all by design, we saw multiple rookies get some playing time on the defense. With Branch injured, Abney II got more playing time, and with Wonnum injured as well, Moore saw an uptick. Rookie defensive tackle Skylar Gill-Howard got his second sack of the season, and Rolder got his first career sack. This defense was injected with youth, primarily through the NFL Draft, and while some players weren’t expected to have a big impact this season, they are showing the coaching staff they deserve to be on the field with the veterans. The offense got younger along the offensive line; despite allowing four sacks on Goff, they helped the running game and Gibbs come alive. This team is showing their window isn’t closed yet; it’s lasting longer with how much young talent is on the team.

title: Lions vs. Vikings recap, highlights: Detroit grinds out win with electric 2nd-half run game
summary: The Detroit Lions offense looked like they had met their match in the first half against the Minnesota Vikings. But in the second half, the Lions came alive with a rushing attack that Minnesota had no answer for. The Lions dropped over 230 rushing yards on the Vikings, with impressive games from both Jahmyr Gibbs […]
full_text: Nov 1, 2026; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs (0) runs during the third quarter against the Minnesota Vikings at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Detroit Lions offense looked like they had met their match in the first half against the Minnesota Vikings. But in the second half, the Lions came alive with a rushing attack that Minnesota had no answer for. The Lions dropped over 230 rushing yards on the Vikings, with impressive games from both Jahmyr Gibbs (153 yards) and Sione Vaki (65 yards). The game was stopped early in the fourth quarter when Lions linebacker Jack Campbell suffered a neck injury and was carted off and taken to a nearby hospital. For updates on Jack Campbell injury status, click here. With the win, the Lions move to 5-2 on the season, just a game behind the no-longer-undefeated Vikings (6-1) in a tight NFC North race. First quarter The Lions won the toss and opted to defer, giving the Vikings offense the opportunity to have the ball first. After a touchback, Kyler Murray connected on a big play to put Minnesota in Lions territory on just one play: tight end Ben Yurosek was wide open for a 24-yard gain. A deep shot to Jordan Addison went incomplete, setting up a third-and-7 from Detroit’s 38-yard line. T.J. Hockenson nearly made a diving catch, but the ball hit the ground, setting up a 57-yard attempt, and Will Reichard pushed it right for his first (non-blocked) miss of the season. Detroit took over at their own 47-yard line after the missed kick. It appeared the Lions were going to go three-and-out, but a roughing the passer penalty extended the drive after Jared Goff failed to connect with Amon-Ra St. Brown on third down. The refs would strike back in the Vikings favor, when after a first down conversion from Sione Vaki, St. Brown was called for taunting, pushing the Lions back toward midfield. Detroit wouldn’t recover, suffering sacks on two of the next three plays, pushing them out of field goal position. Pinned deep in their own zone, the Vikings managed just a single first down on a Jordan Mason 10-yard run. On the ensuing third down, Murray couldn’t find anyone open and chucked it well over Jordan Addison’s head. The Lions got a little bit of luck on their next drive, with a deflected pass from Goff landed into the hands of St. Brown for a ridiculous third-down conversion. Detroit nearly took full advantage. A deep shot to Jameson Williams gained 46 yards, but another taunting penalty pushed Detroit back 15 yards. Big play from Goff to JaMo on 3rd and 12! MINvsDET on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/FLspKRJxqE — NFL (@NFL) November 1, 2026 Detroit nearly found paydirt on the next play, but a 24-yard pass to St. Brown was ruled incomplete upon review when the ball was dislodged after the Lions receiver hit the ground. Amon-Ra St. Brown injury video -In locker room for concussion eval pic.twitter.com/HaWpCpZlrb — Jimmy Liao MD | Detroit Lions Morning Rounds (@JimmyLiaoMD) November 1, 2026 After the play, St. Brown was taken to the locker room, but he returned to play after the drive. Detroit was still able to move toward the goal line, but on third-and-5, Goff, under duress, couldn’t connect with Gibbs, and they settled for a short field goal. 3-0 Lions. The Vikings offense moved into Lions’ territory thanks to a 23-yard pass interference penalty on D.J. Reed. Then Murray found T.J. Hockenson for 22 yards down to the 16-yard line. Second quarter The Vikings would score quickly in the second quarter, after Aaron Jones juked two defenders to turn a negative play into a 15-yard gain. Then, Justin Jefferson caught a 1-yard fade to make it 7-3 Vikings , 35 seconds into the quarter. Justin Jefferson. 1 of 1. MINvsDET on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/oYt9SSvBZI — NFL (@NFL) November 1, 2026 The Lions went nowhere on their next possession. After two runs went for 2 yards, Goff tried to find Williams, but the speedy receiver fell on his route, and the ball went into James Pierre’s hands for Goff’s first interception of the season. James Pierre picks it off! MINvsDET on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XZ8sQnAqCx — NFL (@NFL) November 1, 2026 Minnesota took over at their own 46-yard line, looking to add to their lead. However, they quickly went three-and-out. Murray successfully escaped pressure on third-and-9, but he airmailed a ball to Jefferson. The Vikings successfully pinned the Lions at their own 8-yard line, though, with a nice punt from Brett Thorson. Before the next drive, Lions center Cade Mays was declared questionable to return with an ankle injury. He was eventually ruled OUT. Detroit was able to overcome two early false starts, but their short-yardage run game continued to hurt them. A toss to Jahmyr Gibbs on third-and-1 was blown up in the backfield, and the Lions punted. The Vikings quickly went three-and-out thanks to a second down sack from Skyler Gill-Howard. Sun Bleach got 'em!!! pic.twitter.com/MOiNDpomQe — Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 1, 2026 A shank on the punt gave the Lions the ball at midfield, but Detroit squandered the opportunity. Despite gaining 7 yards on first down, a Gibbs run went -3, and Goff was sacked for the fourth time on third down. Minnesota took over on their own 10-yard line with 3:10 left, hoping to run their two-minute drill. They kicked the drive off with a play-action boot to Jefferson for 7-yards. On the play, Brian Branch friendly-fired on defensive end DJ Wonnum, who was very slow to get up and eventually carted off. Branch also headed to the locker room, likely for a concussion evaluation. The Lions announced that both were being evaluated for concussions, and both were later downgraded to OUT. Murray pushed the Vikings to midfield with a scramble, but he airmailed another pass. This time, D.J. Reed picked it off. DJ Reed laid out for it and got his offense the ball back MINvsDET on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/crH0KuFHuV — NFL (@NFL) November 1, 2026 The Lions made sure to bleed as much clock as possible to leave no time for the Vikings. But they left little time for them to realistically get in the end zone. That said, an offsides from the Vikings kept the drive alive on fourth-and-1, and Williams caught a 14-yard pass to get into field goal range. After a holding penalty pushed them back, Gibbs put them right back in range with a 19-yard gain. Jake Bates drilled it from 37 yards out to make it 7-6 Vikings at halftime. Third quarter The Lions put together a solid drive to open up the second half, mostly consisting of short passes. However, Detroit stalled on a third down when a screen to Williams came up well short. Then Jake Bates doinked a 46-yard field goal off the left upright to keep it 7-6 Vikings. The Vikings couldn’t take advantage, as the Lions got Murray off the field with a pair of quick sacks—one by Alim McNeill and one by rookie linebacker Jimmy Rolder. Detroit’s offense finally broke through on the next drive. Sam LaPorta picked up 19 yards on a checkdown to start the drive, then Gibbs started to come alive with an 11-yard run. On third-and-8, the Lions ran a neat play where St. Brown lined up about 15 yards off the line of scrimmage, then caught a pass with a running start to pick up the first. title: Green Bay Packers News: Ty’Ron Hopper is having his moment
summary: Ty’Ron Hopper was famously a virtually invisible man for his first two years in Green Bay. You’ve heard the numbers, but permit me to recount them again. Over his first two seasons with the Packers, Hopper lined up for just 144 snaps on defense. He played more on special teams, but considering how many of […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - OCTOBER 29: Ty'Ron Hopper #59 of the Green Bay Packers lines up before the snap during an NFL football game against the Carolina Panthers at Lambeau Field on October 29, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ty’Ron Hopper was famously a virtually invisible man for his first two years in Green Bay. You’ve heard the numbers, but permit me to recount them again. Over his first two seasons with the Packers, Hopper lined up for just 144 snaps on defense. He played more on special teams, but considering how many of his reps came on kickoff coverage and return, a good number of those snaps involved him doing literally nothing as the ball sailed into the end zone for a touchback. Prior to injuries to Edgerrin Cooper and Zaire Franklin, there were 21 games in Hopper’s career where he was active but never appeared on defense. In 15 games, he recorded zero tackles — despite being in uniform and on the field, he had the same measurable impact on the game that you or I did. But with those aforementioned injuries clearing the way, Hopper has blossomed. Thursday night he had a remarkable statistical performance, recording multiple passes defensed, an interception, and a sack, an outing only duplicated in recent Packers history by Charles Woodson, which is pretty excellent company to keep. None of this, for what it’s worth, is evidence that Hopper is about to become a core part of the Packers defense. Anybody can have a good game or two; putting together consistently good performances is what separates the metaphorical men from the boys. But this is far more than we’ve seen from Hopper to this point, and, if nothing else, it should be evidence that he can do good things for the defense when he’s on the field. Considering how little he’s been on the field so far, that’s a huge step forward. title: Packers vs. Patriots odds: Opening lines for Week 9 matchup
summary: The Green Bay Packers have opened up as 2.5-point road underdogs on FanDuel against the New England Patriots in Week 9, coming off a mini-bye after beating the Carolina Panthers on Thursday Night Football. The Patriots had a little scare against the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, but were able to outscore Miami 21-6 in the […]
full_text: (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers have opened up as 2.5-point road underdogs on FanDuel against the New England Patriots in Week 9, coming off a mini-bye after beating the Carolina Panthers on Thursday Night Football . The Patriots had a little scare against the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, but were able to outscore Miami 21-6 in the second half to win 24-19. Overall, quarterback Drake Maye seems to have caught his groove after starting slowly to begin the 2026 season. Over the last four games, he’s posted MVP-type numbers, combining to throw 11 touchdowns to just one interception and crossing the 110 passer rating mark in each of those games. The Packers are also coming in relatively hot, mostly off the backs of their defense and offensive passing game, and have won four of their last five games after being embarrassed at home for Thursday Night Football against the Atlanta Falcons. Both teams are fighting for something on Sunday, as the Patriots’ chances of winning the AFC East drop from 31 percent to just 21 percent if the Packers beat them, according to The Athletic’s playoff simulator . Green Bay’s path to the playoffs mostly involves a wild card spot at this point, as the team is being given just a seven percent chance of winning the division per the same simulator. According to The Athletic, the Packers have a 61 percent chance to make the playoffs if they beat the Patriots, but just a 39 percent chance if they lose. If Green Bay can split their trip to New England and their Week 10 game against the Minnesota Vikings, who are sitting in the driver’s seat in the NFC North at the moment, they have about a 50-50 chance of making the playoffs going into their Week 11 bye week. After that, they should be getting some players back from injury lists, notably edge rusher Micah Parsons. Go Pack Go—wherever you go! title: Pro Football Blurry
summary: Pro Football Focus has always had a few understandable issues with subjectivity. Grades are not hard and fast metrics, and they can occasionally be wrong as a result; however, I do believe PFF’s goals were both honorable and valuable. It is incredibly difficult to separate out performances in football, as running backs are only as […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Pro Football Focus has always had a few understandable issues with subjectivity. Grades are not hard and fast metrics, and they can occasionally be wrong as a result; however, I do believe PFF’s goals were both honorable and valuable. It is incredibly difficult to separate out performances in football, as running backs are only as good as the lines blocking for them, and even good corners can appear terrible without some semblance of a pass rush in front of them. PFF attempted to leverage time-tested scouting processes to rank individual players regardless of their surroundings. I can already hear people, including younger versions of myself, yelling that PFF has always been bad, but that’s really not true. Ben Baldwin, who helped to develop much of that analytics framework available to the public on advanced stats like EPA and CPOE, and who maintains RBSDM.com used to run statistical analysis of PFF’s quarterback grades versus more objective statistics, and PFF grades would generally come out on top in terms of predictive value, or at least very close too it. And for positions like offensive line, where traditional stats don’t even really exist, PFF grades have always been useful, or at least better than nothing. But several years ago, PFF’s focus started to move away from the consumer-facing side of the house, and it sure seems as if their grades have gotten less attached to reality. Now, just because I think a grade is bad doesn’t mean the grade is necessarily bad. I’m certainly not anything close to perfect at this whole football thing. But we’re also starting to see some consistency issues within PFF itself, where their own internal statistical tracking really disagrees with the grading. The most obvious example on the Packer side of things is Dani Dennis-Sutton , who is having a sensational rookie campaign, especially for a fourth-rounder. DDS has recorded 20 total pressures on just 143 pass-rushing snaps. The raw total ties him at 24 th overall out of 150 qualifiers , and the only players who have more pressures in fewer snaps are Trey Hendrickson and Green Bay’s Brenton Cox. DDS also ranks highly in hurries, and he’s also only one of thirteen edge rushers with a pass broken up on the season. Despite all of this, his 60.4 pass rushing grade is just 87 th , and his overall grade is barely better. If you wanted to argue that DDS gives up some value on run defense, I am perfectly willing to believe you, but having him in the middle of the pack on pass rush is insanity. We here at Acme Packing Company pay special attention to Dennis-Sutton as he was the rare draft crush that actually ended up on the team , but we’re not exactly biased in terms of calling out Packer players when they are terrible players or people . Another recent example is linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper’s grade from the Panther’s game on Thursday . Hopper is in for the injured Zaire Franklin and/or Edgerrin Cooper, and frankly, many of us didn’t think much of Hopper entering the game. He was great in every facet on Thursday; he filled up the stat sheet with a pick, a sack, and three passes defended. He was a monster. He was also the third-lowest-graded Packer defender ahead of only Javon Bullard and Carrington Valentine. Sometimes interceptions are lucky and just fall into your hands, but Hopper was in great coverage positions several times, a sure tackler, and most importantly for an off-ball linebacker, he showed incredible versatility. And yes, stats can be deceiving, but please check out this breakdown of his play by Tyler Brooke for an explanation of why the stats were, in fact, dead on. I might be willing to listen to an argument that Hopper was just average and benefitted from the efforts of those around him. I still think that’s wrong, and that he was one of the best players on the field, but I would get it. Arguing that he was the third-worst Packer defender is ridiculous. And that’s the problem in a nutshell. A good model will return results that are 80% exactly what you think they should be, and 10-20% surprises (that you need to double-check). If it’s too far off, the model is probably broken. I think we’ve reached a point where things are getting a bit too far off. PFF also says that Tyler Shough and Geno Smith have been better than Jordan Love (AND Caleb Williams) , with Love as the 15 th overall QB and Williams at 13. Love’s statistics are down this year and based purely on numbers, ranking him 15 th is somewhat justified, but the PFF ethos is supposed to be about seeing the Packers’ offensive line for what it is and giving the poor guy some extra credit. At this point, I’m not really sure what value PFF grades are adding. It’s a shame.
author: Paul Noonan

title: Packers Film Room: Jordan Love throws 3 TDs
summary: While an interception is a black mark on the stat line, Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love turned in a nice day. With no run game to speak of (their running backs carried the ball 25 times for 48 yards, a whopping 1.9 yards per carry), Love was the engine that kept the offense moving, […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images While an interception is a black mark on the stat line, Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love turned in a nice day. With no run game to speak of (their running backs carried the ball 25 times for 48 yards, a whopping 1.9 yards per carry), Love was the engine that kept the offense moving, going 30/41 (73.2%) for 288 yards, 3 TDs and 1 INT for a QB rating of 106.6 and an EPA per Dropback of +0.11. Today, we’re going to break down his 3 touchdown passes. Play 1: 3rd & 8, 5:12 remaining in the 1st quarter The Packers are in 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR). They start in a 2×2 set, but Christian Watson [9] shifts to the left before the snap, leaving Tucker Kraft [85] as the lone receiver on the line on the right side (with Josh Jacobs [8] aligned in the backfield on the same side of the formation). Devin Lloyd [55] bumps over with the shift from Watson, but no one follows him, indicating that the Panthers are likely in zone coverage. They’re showing two-high safeties before the snap, in what would be a Middle Field Open coverage (based on the position of the corners, they’re showing a Quarters look). Jacobs does a little shuffle motion at the snap, slightly moving the defenders on the right side over. On the right side of the field, Jacobs is running an out route and Kraft is running up the seam. Love is reading the safeties after the snap to see if they rotate or if the middle of the field stays open. After the ball is snapped the safeties stay in a two-high alignment. Kraft slightly bends his route to the outside to get the safety leaning to the outside, then bends back inside. With the middle field open, Love just needs to make sure the linebacker can’t drop under. Bobby Okereke [58] is originally aligned as an edge rusher, but drops back into zone at the snap. Kraft is bending over the top, but Love can’t stare it down. He has his feet and shoulders pointed to the outside, then opens up and fires to the middle. With Okereke drifting outside and Kraft bending back in, Love unleashes a bullet to split the safeties and take a 6-3 lead. Here’s that throw in slow motion, just because. Play 2: 3rd & 13, 1:51 remaining in the 2nd quarter The Packers are in 11 personnel, in a 3×1 set (with Kraft the lone receiver on the line on the right side). This is the play directly after Matthew Golden [0] dropped a TD on a Huggo (they’re 1-for-3 on those this year). On the next play, Love goes right back to him. They’re running a deep Smash variant, with Golden running the corner route from the #3 receiver spot. The Panthers have a lot of bodies at the line, leaving a lot of air in the coverage over Trip. They’ve got two defenders aligned deep over the outside receivers, and the deep safety over Golden (15 yards down the field). Golden looks back at Love a few steps off the line, in case there’s a Hot throw coming. I like seeing that from Golden. With no throw, Golden pushes vertically and Zakee Wheatley [20] drifts to the middle to protect the post. That gives Golden some really nice inside leverage. J. Michael Sturdivant [87] is running a Deep Out route from the #2 spot. When he cuts to the corner, he brings Tre’Von Moehrig [7] with him, opening a space over the top. If Love leads Golden up the field, it would give Moehrig a chance to catch up and get his hands on the ball. With so much room on the inside, Love lays this ball up, allowing Golden to make the catch and get into the end zone without either safety being able to touch him. Play 3: 3rd & 1, 7:34 remaining in the 3rd quarter Facing 3rd & 1 inside the 5-yard line, the Packers come out in 12 personnel (1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR). They’re in empty, with Josh Jacobs [8] acting as the TE on the left side of the line, with Golden aligned outside. They’re showing a heavy look on the right, with both TEs on the line and J. Michael Sturdivant in a tight split. The two defenders over Golden and Jacobs are in a stack. At the time, it’s tough to tell what coverage they’ll be playing. They’re going to be in Man coverage, but, down here, it’s quite possible that they’ll Banjo the coverage (switch coverage assignments if there is a switch release). At the snap, Golden pushes vertically while Jacobs releases with an outside angle. The inside defender (Okereke) hops over Golden to pick up Jacobs, so they’re in straight man assignments. That’s perfect. By jumping over the push from Golden, he is now overcommitted to the outside. When Jacobs cuts back inside on an Angle route, there’s nothing really to be done about it. Love puts it on Jacobs and Jacobs uses his body to shield the ball from Okereke. Albums listened to: Michael Nau – Popfly ; John Carpenter – Halloween [Soundtrack] ; Alex G – Camp Miasma [Score] ; Disasterpeace – It Follows [Soundtrack]

title: Value of Things: In the rearview mirror
summary: Some of you are undoubtedly confused at the title. The Texans are coming off of a bye week, so what exactly are we looking at in the rearview mirror? Well, this is what we would lovingly call self-scouting. We are looking at the Texans season rankings in the various categories to see if we can […]
full_text: Feb 2, 2023; Houston, TX, USA; Houston Texans head coach Demeco Ryans speaks to the media during his introductory press conference at NRG Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Erik Williams-USA TODAY Sports Some of you are undoubtedly confused at the title. The Texans are coming off of a bye week, so what exactly are we looking at in the rearview mirror? Well, this is what we would lovingly call self-scouting. We are looking at the Texans season rankings in the various categories to see if we can identify key points that they will need to improve on for the rest of the season, Obviously, if you are 2-5 on the season then there are definitely some things to improve on. However, not all 2-5 football teams are created equal. Teams like the Dolphins and Titans repeatedly (although not the last two weeks) get their doors blown off. The Chargers have been an absolute mess and I am watching two dreadful teams on Sunday night football as I type this. The Texans are minus seven points in point differential which would seem to predict a 3-4 or even 4-3 record in some instances. So, clearly it is not completely awful. So, the numbers we look at could be the beginning of figuring out a way around this. The team is 1-4 in one score games. Maybe some better luck is coming their way in the second half. Maybe there is one key adjustment they can make on either side of the ball to turn their fortunes around. The main thing is that the record really doesn’t accurately tell us what is going on with this football team. Key Numbers Total Yards: Offense 2367/13, Defense 2394/22 Rushing Yards: Offense 593/29, Defense 686/16 Passing Yards: Offense 1774/6, Defense 1708/29 Penalties: 58/508 (30th) Sacks: Offense 15 (17th). Defense 21 (2nd) Turnovers: Offense 3 (2nd), Defense 6 (26th) Points per game: Offense 23.6 (15th), Defense 24.3 (19th) Obviously, many of these numbers cut both ways, but there are a few that stand out when we get to the good, bad, and ugly on the season. We usually do great, good, and bad in victory, but with the team 2-5 victory doesn’t feel like the way to go. I should point out that they are mostly even in total yards and passing yards. They are in the positive on the plus/minus. It almost seems like they are finding creative ways to lose football games. This feels like a .500 team and that is where you would think they would end up. The Good We will actually get to C.J. Stroud later in the week, so we will not say too much on him in this space. However, there has been growth in the passing game in general. The team had some finds in the draft and free agency in terms of skill position players. Jaylin Noel looked a lot better before he went down with a season ending injury. Foster Moreau was a really good addition as a secondary tight end. We should remember this when we are levying our complaints about free agent signings and draft picks gone wrong. Not everything is negative and not everything is positive. Most seasons have both in somewhat equal measure. The difference would be the sheer number of injuries the Texans have sustained on both sides of the ball and there is little that can be done about that. The Bad A very significant part of me feels sorry for Nick Caley. For the last year and a half he has been the most convenient whipping boy for the fanbase and those of us at BRB have certainly participated in that whipping and I might be the most guilty party. This is where we point out that they have surrendered the second fewest turnovers in the NFL and are in the middle of the pack in points per game and total yards. So, whether or not you torch Caley depends largely on whether you are looking at it from 10,000 feet or five feet. The closer you look the more cracks you see in the veneer. You begin to notice one of the worst rushing attacks in the NFL. You notice an offense that looks dead at key points in games after the opposing polo has managed to scheme up something to stop the offense. Caley is just not good at adjusting on the fly. He can’t draw up a third and one play to save his life. These are things you can’t necessarily see when you look at just the aggregate data. Maybe even more importantly, we notice that key changes to personnel seem to come too late or not at all. David Montgomery was clearly inferior to Woody Marks, but stayed in the starting lineup until he was hurt. Xavier Hutchinso is still getting snaps over Marvin Harrison Jr. and was getting them over Jaylin Noel for much of the season. Maybe even more glaring, Keelan Rutledge is one of the lowest rated guards in the NFL according to PFF, but a superior Wyatt Teller is waiting on the bench. Evan Brown is one of the bottom five centers in the NFL and only a couple that could be called starters are listed below him. Part of this is on Nick Caserio for the players he gives to Caley. However, the other part is on Caley for not recognizing that certain guys needed to be replaced in the lineup. I know you don’t want to kill Rutledge’s confidence, but there comes a point when the best five guys need to be out there. More than anything, this probably goes to DeMeco Ryans more than anything. This isn’t a smash mouth running football team. It hasn’t been that at any time during Ryans’ tenure. I get that this is what he wants and that makes perfect sense, but at some point you need to go with what you are. You are a spread em’ out passing football team. You might as well lean into that. The Ugly The words we just said about the offense could be echoed about the defense. The main difference is that the defense was supposed to be a top five unit in the NFL. They certainly have not been that with the exception of the Tennessee Titans game. I could certainly write off the Jacksonville game to the field conditions or the Buffalo and Cincinnati game to playing top five quarterbacks in the league. There comes a certain point when you run out of excuses. There are three problems that we can isolate with the defense. The first is a lack of turnovers. Six turnovers through seven games is simply not good enough. That could be a function of performance, but it is probably more a factor of luck. Sometimes the bounces just don’t go your way. Still, there were a couple of prominent opportunities for picks that would have turned two losses into wins. A 4-3 start certainly looks a lot better than 2-5. The second problem is the same as above. Reed Blankenship is dead ass last in safeties according to PFF. I would say that we would be surprised, but PFF also rated him as one of the worst safeties last year. Somehow Caserio thought he was a good guy to sign anyway. Add in the fact that some other players (almost all in the secondary) have not played good football this year and you have the makings of a disappointing defense regardless of scheme. That brings us to scheme. The Texans have played more lax and more bend but don’t break defense. The obvious reason was to avoid big plays, but they still have given up a ton of big plays. They rely on the front four to get home and they do more often than most teams, but they need to have more consistent pressure. More importantly, they used to make life miserable for quarterbacks. Things have been way too easy for them this season. Ryans may not want to consider personnel changes or scheme changes, but after seven weeks the “it’s early” mantra just isn’t going to fly.

I think that when a fan is unable to sustain in their needed amount of BIRG (basking in reflected glory), they begin to adopt other means of getting the same feeling; good old-fashioned schaudenfreude. title: Houston Texans Updated Wide Receiver Room
summary: The Houston Texans took a hit to their wide receiver room this past Sunday, losing Jaylin Noel to a turf toe injury that will end his season. Noel started off slow but really began to hit his stride, looking like one of the most explosive wide receivers in the league during that stretch. Houston went […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - DECEMBER 21: Tank Dell #3 of the Houston Texans looks on from the sideline during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Kansas City Chiefs at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium on December 21, 2024 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Houston Texans took a hit to their wide receiver room this past Sunday, losing Jaylin Noel to a turf toe injury that will end his season. Noel started off slow but really began to hit his stride, looking like one of the most explosive wide receivers in the league during that stretch. Houston went from having a lackluster wide receiver room to an unbelievably loaded one in a matter of weeks, and now they have suffered another loss at the position. The good news is that they still have more than capable receivers, and there should not be a major drop-off, especially with how quarterback C.J. Stroud has been playing this season. General manager Nick Caserio made a major move earlier this year, acquiring Marvin Harrison Jr. from the Arizona Cardinals. Harrison has already made an impact despite limited opportunities as he continues learning the offense. After the bye week, his snap count should increase significantly, and he will provide another talented option alongside Nico Collins. Another player who will need to step up is Tank Dell, who recently returned after nearly two years away from football. He played very little in his first game back but was able to haul in a reception and take it over 40 yards, providing a much-needed spark to the offense. His chemistry with Stroud is still there, and as he continues working his way back, he will bring an explosive element to an offense that needs it. After those three, Houston still has Kayshon Boutte and Xavier Hutchinson, who provide excellent depth. Both players have stepped up at different points throughout the season. The Texans’ offense should have no problem moving the ball through the air, but they still have plenty of work to do with their rushing attack to provide more balance and make the unit even better.

title: Which Colts players should still matter by 2029?
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are in a difficult position, and after Sunday’s humiliating 42-7 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars, it’s becoming increasingly clear that the franchise is much further away from contention than many originally believed. At 2-6, with Chris Ballard having already been fired and two of the organization’s most accomplished players traded away, Indianapolis […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - SEPTEMBER 20: Tyler Warren #84 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates a touchdown with Matt Goncalves #71 in the first quarter of an NFL game between the Indianapolis Colts and Kansas City Chiefs on Sep 20, 2026 at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts are in a difficult position, and after Sunday’s humiliating 42-7 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars, it’s becoming increasingly clear that the franchise is much further away from contention than many originally believed. At 2-6, with Chris Ballard having already been fired and two of the organization’s most accomplished players traded away, Indianapolis appears headed toward another significant rebuilding period. Unfortunately, this may not be a particularly quick turnaround. The Colts have already surrendered their 2027 first-round pick in the Sauce Gardner trade, and with several established veterans approaching free agency or the later stages of their careers, there is a legitimate argument that Indianapolis will struggle to compete next season as well. Even if the organization manages to find its next franchise quarterback in 2028, expecting that player to immediately transform the team into a contender would be unrealistic. With that in mind, I’m looking at 2029 as the first reasonable target for Indianapolis to become a legitimately competitive team again. That doesn’t mean the Colts cannot improve before then, but building a roster capable of consistently competing with the NFL’s best will require several successful drafts, meaningful player development and a much clearer long-term plan from whoever takes over as general manager. So rather than evaluating who deserves to start for the Colts today, I wanted to examine which players currently on the roster could realistically contribute to a winning team in 2029. Just as importantly, what roles should those players occupy? Someone might be a starter in Indianapolis right now but only qualify as a rotational player on a Super Bowl contender. Others could become genuine building blocks who remain with the franchise for the next several years. Age, contracts, performance and potential development all factor into these evaluations. I’ve separated 50 players into five categories, ranging from established players worth building around to those who likely won’t be part of the organization’s next competitive window. The projected ages refer approximately to the 2029 season, while several players would need extensions or new contracts to remain with Indianapolis by then. 1. Build around them These are the players I believe could hold legitimate starting roles on a competitive Colts team in 2029. Some are already among the best at their positions, while others are young enough to develop into important long-term contributors. Sauce Gardner — CB1 | Age 29 in 2029 Gardner is arguably the easiest player to include in this category. The Colts invested two first-round selections to acquire him from the New York Jets, and his four-year, $120.4 million extension runs through the 2030 season. While injuries have limited him at times, he remains one of the NFL’s premier cover corners and should still be performing at a high level in 2029. Indianapolis has already committed significant resources to making him a cornerstone of its defense, and barring a dramatic decline, Gardner should remain the team’s No. 1 cornerback throughout its next competitive window. Tyler Warren — TE1 | Age 27 Warren is another relatively straightforward selection. The former first-round pick has already demonstrated the versatility and receiving ability necessary to become one of the league’s better tight ends, and he should be entering his physical prime by 2029. His rookie contract runs through 2028, with Indianapolis holding a fifth-year option for 2029. Given his potential, I would expect the Colts to exercise that option if he continues developing as anticipated. Warren could become a foundational piece of the next offense, particularly if Indianapolis finally finds a long-term answer at quarterback. Bernhard Raimann — LT1 | Age 32 Raimann has experienced a somewhat disappointing 2026 season by the standards he established over the previous few years, but that shouldn’t erase the fact that he remains a quality starting left tackle. Indianapolis signed him to a four-year, $100 million extension running through 2029, providing valuable stability at one of the NFL’s most important positions. Although Raimann will be entering his early 30s by then, offensive tackles can remain effective well beyond that age, and there is little reason to believe the Colts should be looking for his replacement anytime soon. He might not be among the five best tackles in football, but he’s more than capable of protecting the blind side of a quarterback on a winning team. Alec Pierce — WR2 | Age 29 Pierce received a substantial four-year, $114 million extension during the 2026 offseason, meaning Indianapolis has already committed to keeping him around through 2029. His combination of size, speed and downfield ability makes him a valuable offensive weapon, although I believe his ideal role on a genuinely competitive team is as a complementary No. 2 receiver rather than the primary receiving option. Pierce can stretch defenses vertically and create explosive plays, but the Colts would benefit from eventually finding a more complete WR1 who can consistently win in multiple areas of the field. That would allow Pierce to focus on the strengths that make him such a dangerous player. Adetomiwa Adebawore — DT1 (3-technique) | Age 28 Adebawore might be the most exciting developmental piece on the Colts’ defensive line. His athleticism and ability to generate interior pressure have become increasingly apparent, particularly following his recent two-sack performance against Minnesota. With DeForest Buckner now in San Francisco, Adebawore has an opportunity to establish himself as the organization’s long-term starter at the three-technique position. However, his rookie contract expires after this season, making an extension an immediate priority. If Indianapolis can retain him and his development continues, he has the potential to become one of the defense’s most disruptive players by 2029. CJ Allen — MLB1 | Age 24 Allen is one of the few players on the roster who could still be several years away from reaching his prime when the Colts are ready to compete again. The 2026 second-round pick has started showing encouraging signs in recent weeks, demonstrating the instincts, physicality and range necessary to eventually become a reliable starting middle linebacker. His rookie contract runs through 2029, providing Indianapolis with a young defensive player who should still be relatively inexpensive during the proposed competitive window. While it’s far too early to call him a star, Allen has shown enough to make me comfortable projecting him as the long-term MIKE linebacker, assuming his development continues. Matt Goncalves — RG1 | Age 28 Goncalves has quietly developed into one of the more dependable young players on the offensive line and looks capable of holding down the starting right guard position for years to come. His rookie contract expires after the 2027 season, meaning Indianapolis would need to negotiate a second deal to retain him through 2029. Given his age, versatility and improvement since arriving in the league, that should be a priority if his performance remains consistent. The Colts have already lost Quenton Nelson and cannot afford to keep replacing quality offensive linemen. Goncalves may never reach Nelson’s level, but he has the potential to become a long-term starter on a competitive offensive line. Cam Bynum — FS1 | Age 31 Bynum is somewhat different from the younger players in this category because he will be entering his 30s by the time Indianapolis is ready to…

title: That performance from the Colts was as bad as it gets
summary: Ugly. That is the best and most PG word I can think of to describe what we witnessed on Sunday in Jacksonville. That is if “we” even watched that game. Maybe you tuned in out of curiosity in the first quarter, but if you stuck around from beginning to end, you are stronger than I […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 1: Wide receiver Parker Washington #11 of the Jacksonville Jaguars runs for a first down in the second quarter against the Indianapolis Colts at EverBank Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ugly. That is the best and most PG word I can think of to describe what we witnessed on Sunday in Jacksonville. That is if “we” even watched that game. Maybe you tuned in out of curiosity in the first quarter, but if you stuck around from beginning to end, you are stronger than I am. That was rough. A shattered franchise must now pick up the pieces and figure out what to do. The Indianapolis Colts weren’t just bad on Sunday; they were horrific. It definitely fit the vibe of Halloween weekend because it was downright terrifying. 28-0 was the score at halftime as a fumble and an interception returned for a touchdown led the way. Tyler Warren had four receptions on ten targets for 18 yards. Ouch . One of them bounced off him and into the arms of a Jags defender who took it to the house. That was the last moment, if there were any before, that one might have thought this team had any fight left. Daniel Jones is barely throwing the ball downfield. His 144 yards isn’t going to cut it. Actually, it didn’t, as Anthony Richardson came into the game late. Was it because of the blowout, or is there something more? Rumors are starting to swirl that the Colts might make a change. Swapping quarterbacks won’t fix this defense, though. The tackling and coverage were atrocious. This is Chris Ballard’s roster, ladies and gentlemen. The roster is being picked over like a carcass on the side of the road. The effort is seemingly gone, and other teams are set to feast. As bad as it is, it might get worse. The Colts are back to no viable quarterback, a place where Chris Ballard has had this team for years. They don’t have a first-round pick either. I’m not sure if the Colts have hit rock bottom yet, but it sure is dark. I don’t want to see where they go from here.

title: Colts-Cowboys opening odds: Colts are falling fast
summary: The Indianapolis Colts return home after a brutal two-game road trip. The Colts just completed their annual beatdown at the hands of the Jaguars and are hoping home has some better results. The Cowboys are licking their own wounds and will be in fight mode to save their season. FanDuel Sportsbook is giving the Cowboys […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 26: Detail view of a Dallas Cowboys helmet prior to an NFL football game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on October 26, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts return home after a brutal two-game road trip. The Colts just completed their annual beatdown at the hands of the Jaguars and are hoping home has some better results. The Cowboys are licking their own wounds and will be in fight mode to save their season. FanDuel Sportsbook is giving the Cowboys all the love as the Colts are 5.5-point underdogs. The money line is +220 and the over/under is 52.5. What is there to say? Going on the road against the Jaguars has been the Colts’ kryptonite. Before things kicked off, it didn’t seem like this was the year the losing streak was going to end. All that game ended was a few more players’ careers as Colts. Turnovers, missed tackles, and a team that looks like it has thrown in the towel was on the field this week. It was 35-0 before the Colts decided to score. That’s all you really need to know about this one. Dallas seemed to have their high-scoring affair under wraps with less than four minutes left in the fourth. Up ten wasn’t enough, however, as the Cardinals scored a game-tying touchdown with ten seconds left. They gave the Cowboys a gift by missing the extra point and sending this one into overtime. Both teams got a possession in overtime, but the Cardinals got the last laugh with a game-winning field goal. Neither team is feeling good about their season. Dallas still has hope though. Expect Lucas Oil to be full of Cowboys fans as they travel well, and the Colts fans might have already thrown in the towel. If the Colts are going to get things right, it has to be this one. If not here, it might not happen this year at all.
author: Jon Spradley

title: Colts hit rock bottom in humiliating 12th straight road loss to Jaguars
summary: If you want to witness an unmitigated disaster, buckle up and watch the Indianapolis Colts play football in Jacksonville. Seriously, don’t turn it off.  The Colts gave into their annual humiliation ritual, losing 42-7 to the Jaguars at EverBank Stadium. The latest loss extended the road losing streak against their AFC South rival to 12 consecutive […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 1: Safety Jalen Huskey #22 of the Jacksonville Jaguars sacks quarterback Anthony Richardson #5 of the Indianapolis Colts in the fourth quarter at EverBank Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images If you want to witness an unmitigated disaster, buckle up and watch the Indianapolis Colts play football in Jacksonville. Seriously, don’t turn it off. The Colts gave into their annual humiliation ritual, losing 42-7 to the Jaguars at EverBank Stadium. The latest loss extended the road losing streak against their AFC South rival to 12 consecutive games as Indianapolis has not won in Jacksonville since 2014, back when Barack Obama was still the President of the United States. 12 years later, the Colts waited until Halloween weekend to visit their house of horrors. There was no fight, no identity. The most obvious decision made was quarterback Daniel Jones getting benched in garbage time. Indianapolis was outclassed in every phase of the game, surrendering four touchdowns in the first half. The final score was ugly, but the on field performance should have yielded a running clock. The first offensive snap offered a brief showcase for star running back Jonathan Taylor to rip off an explosive 19-yard run to stretch the field. The seventh-year tailback is listed on the trading block after rushing for a season-low 23 yards on eight carries. The next seven offensive plays and two drives produced a combined three yards as Indianapolis punted on five of its first six true drives in the first half. Taylor and Josh Downs coughed up a fumble on the lone drive that didn’t result in conceding a punt. Instead of a punt, it was a cartoonish double reverse passing play that handed that ball right back to the Jaguars four plays after their own turnover. What on Earth could be the excuse for this trick play call and execution on first down? The trick play goes awry and the Jaguars get it back! INDvsJAX on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/AinguLvhQi — NFL (@NFL) November 1, 2026 Jacksonville responded with a 12-play, 103-yard opening drive that began at the Jaguars’ own 2-yard line, but the stampede couldn’t get off the field. The Jaguars opening drive was ignited on a 46-yard completion to tight end Brenton Strange that flip the field before quarterback Trevor Lawrence connected with receiver Brian Thomas Jr. for a 12-yard touchdown to take a lead they would never relinquish. The Colts’ offense continued to sleepwalk through the motions as the Jaguars pounced into the end zone four times. Lawrence found tight end Nate Boerkircher for a 31-yard touchdown after the lost fumble, stretching Jacksonville’s lead to 14-0. With under two minutes remaining in the first half, running back Bhayshul Tuten ripped through the heart of Indy’s defense and broke through three tackles for a 39-yard rushing touchdown. The only encouraging moment of the first half came as defensive end Jaylahn Tuimoloau shed the chip, then beat his blocker with an inside move before he strip-sacked Lawrence. Rookie edge rusher Caden Curry recovered the fumble to seize possession in Jacksonville territory and give the offense a chance to cut into the 21-point deficit. Instead, with 25 seconds remaining before halftime, Jones targeted tight end Tyler Warren, but the timing of the throw was slightly early, while the route was slightly slower than expected. The pass tipped off the hands of Warren and was intercepted by Rayuan Lane III, who sprinted 92 yards for a pick-six. Jacksonville went into the locker room with an insurmountable edge as the Colts had handed the Jaguars a touchdown out of sheer incompetence. Whatever was said at halftime clearly did not matter for a coach who seems to be a lame duck on the flight back to Indy. The Colts found the end zone midway through the third quarter, putting together their only respectable offensive drive of 13 plays. Jones connected with receiver Laquon Treadwell over the middle for 18 yards. The offense caught a brief rhythm as Jones hit Taylor out of the backfield for 15 yards, then found Warren for 10 more yards before rookie Seth McGowan bulldozed his way for a 16-yard run. Jones found Downs wide open in the corner of the end zone for a six-yard touchdown to salvage the shutout. Josh Downs gets the Colts on the board in the third 📺CBS & Paramount+ pic.twitter.com/MjQV1HStMG — NFL on CBS 🏈 (@NFLonCBS) November 1, 2026 It was a nice sequence, but hardly something worth celebrating when the team was already trailing by five touchdowns. Jacksonville answered with another scoring drive, finished off with a 25-yard touchdown reception by Tuten from Lawrence. The Colts defense allowed six plays of 25 or more yards, while just one play from the offense went for more than 20. Jones completed 19-of-28 passes for 144 passing yards and one touchdown, but threw two interceptions before Steichen turned to backup QB Anthony Richardson Sr. to start the final frame. Richardson completed both of his passes for just eight yards, which matched his passing production over the last two seasons. There were a couple rookies who stood out, while buried underneath the wreckage. Rookie linebacker CJ Allen collected 10 tackles and his first career sack, delivering his most productive outing of the season. Tuimoloau forced a fumble and Caden Curry recovered it. McGowan added 29 rushing yards on five carries, finishing with more rushing yards than Taylor. CJ ALLEN SACK 💥 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/xAJPPMu9qg — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) November 1, 2026 The front office deserves its own share of the blame based on the decision to commit to Jones with an $88 million contract extension following a season-ending Achilles injury. The acquisition of Sauce Gardner was supposed to transform the broken secondary from last season, but the price Indy paid is not worth it when Gardner’s inability to catch turns takeaways into solid, but frustrating pass breakups. Gardner recorded two pass breakups Sunday but could not fetch the game-changing turnover this defense desperately needs to be able to win, let alone compete. The Colts have reached rock bottom before, but Sunday’s punishing loss was another reminder that there might not be a floor if Taylor is traded away before the trade deadline. Expect more creative ways to disappoint the stampede sporting blue each Sunday, but this pathetic performance in Duval County must have reached the lowest level of embarrassment for an owner who decides to take hand-written notes on the sidelines. Indianapolis hosts the struggling Dallas Cowboys next Sunday inside Lucas Oil Stadium, with kickoff scheduled for 1 p.m.

title: Indianapolis Colts discussion: Week 8 live chat during the Jaguars game
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are on the road to take on the Jacksonville Jaguars for week 8 of the 2026 season, kickoff is at 1:00 p.m. EST. It sure feels like last week’s loss to the Minnesota Vikings happened a lot longer than a week ago. The team traded away franchise cornerstone players Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner. […]
full_text: Nov 10,2023; Frankfurt, Germany; Indianapolis Colts mascot Blue looks on during a fan event at Chicago Meatpackers before an International Series game against the New England Patriots. Mandatory Credit: Nathan Ray Seebeck-USA TODAY Sports | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The Indianapolis Colts are on the road to take on the Jacksonville Jaguars for week 8 of the 2026 season, kickoff is at 1:00 p.m. EST. It sure feels like last week’s loss to the Minnesota Vikings happened a lot longer than a week ago. The team traded away franchise cornerstone players Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner. More rumors swirled about other longtime Colts like Jonathan Taylor and Josh Downs. And as much as some of us would like, there’s no conceivable way the Colts will trade Daniel Jones, sorry. Despite the last week feeling like a month, it has only been seven days and that means the Indianapolis Colts will play another football game today. Today they have the first place Jacksonville Jaguars, who should heavily defeat our Colts. But it’s the NFL anything can happen once the whistle blows, but most likely Indy will be extending their losing streak in Jacksonville for another year. Side Note: I told you about this last week but I’m probably going to keep reminding you each week because I think it’s important for everyone who enjoys these gameday threads. The SB Nation app makes commenting, especially in these game feeds, so much easier. At this point I roll my eyes every time someone asks me to download another app, but this one really does improve the experience so much that even I am telling you that if you like to hang out here, chat, celebrate, commiserate, and argue in the comments, this app is actually worth your time. Links are directly below. Join Stampede Blue on game day! Stay on top of every Colts update and debate every snap with other diehard fans. Game-day discussion is smoother in the SB Nation app. Fewer ads Jump easily between conversations Faster commenting and posting Download on iOS or Android . So what do we have to look forward to? Well I’m not sure about you but today I’m going to be focused on rookie starting left guard Jalen Farmer. Farmer will take the place in the lineup of Seahawks guard Quenton Nelson. I expect to see a lot of ups and downs but hopefully some promising play for the future of the Colts offensive line. Defensively I’m hoping to see C.J. Allen make his first start. Reports were that he was slated to start last weeks game against the Vikings before hurting his ankle. He seems good to go for this week, so hopefully they leave the kid out, sink or swim. I’m also excited to see how Adetomiwa Adebawore looks in an expanded role, with San Francisco 49ers DT DeForest Bucker out of town. Adebawore leads the team with 4 sacks on the season (yes that’s a problem but I’m not talking about that right now) and he’s done it while playing just 36% of the team’s defensive snaps. His production will not scale with his playing time (I mean if it did we would be watching something truly special) but it will be great to see what this man has for this year and the future. One thing I am pretty sure of, Adetomiwa Adebawore is playing his way into a very large contract in 2027 and beyond. Sorry I didn’t spend much time talking about the game itself, it’s probably going to go bad. No one is getting fired. The fire sale will continue. The season’s not halfway over. There’s still so much more suffering to do. Prediction: Jaguars: 26 Colts: 13 As always, go Colts. Per usual, Matt Taylor (play-by-play), Charles Arbuckle (analyst), and Larra Overton (sideline) will be on the call. Regarding those Sirius XM national radio subscribers, Colts fans can listen in on Channel 265 (car radio) and Channel 813 (Sirius XM app). title: 5 Questions with Big Cat Country: A New Era?
summary: In Week 8 of 2026 our Indianapolis Colts will travel to the sunshine state to take on the Jacksonville Jaguars. Knowing the party was hitting the road, I sat down with Gus Logue of Big Cat Country. We swapped questions and answers about both the Jaguars and Colts and what follows is what I’ve learned […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - DECEMBER 07: Tim Patrick #17 of the Jacksonville Jaguars makes a catch for a touchdown defended by Jaylon Jones #40 of the Indianapolis Colts during the second quarter at EverBank Stadium on December 07, 2025 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images In Week 8 of 2026 our Indianapolis Colts will travel to the sunshine state to take on the Jacksonville Jaguars. Knowing the party was hitting the road, I sat down with Gus Logue of Big Cat Country . We swapped questions and answers about both the Jaguars and Colts and what follows is what I’ve learned about this week’s enemy. You can find my answers to his questions here. Chris Shepherd: How are Jaguars fans feeling about their postseason chances sitting at 4-2 with a firm lead on the AFC South? Is this team a contender or do they just play in the AFCS? Gus Logue: I don’t think opinions in Jacksonville have changed much since before the season began. Of course, playing in the AFC South is a nice boost, but the Jaguars are clearly a top-10 or so team in the NFL right now. We’re just not yet sure whether this roster has hit its ceiling, which is a good thing, but one thing that could hold Jacksonville back from being a legitimate Super Bowl contender is its trench play. LT Anton Harrison was just lost for the season due to a knee injury, and every Jags fan is clamoring for pass rush help before the trade deadline. If the OL and DL can take a jump over the second half of the season, the league should really watch out for Jacksonville — and even if that doesn’t happen, Trevor Lawrence and Travis Hunter could still take this team far. Chris Shepherd: If you were an offensive coordinator tasked with creating a game plan to beat this Jaguars defense, what would it look like? Anyone you would target? Anyone you would avoid? Gus Logue: I would target the safety position in general. Antonio Johnson is quietly among Jacksonville’s best defensive players, but he’s been ruled out for Sunday’s game with an ankle injury. No. 2 safety Eric Murray had a concussion a few weeks ago and No. 3 safety Caleb Ransaw is on injured reserve. Very few rushers have been able to reach the second level of Jacksonville’s run defense, so in order to attack this undermanned secondary, I would put the ball in my quarterback’s hands and have him attack the middle of the field. Just don’t throw it to #12. Chris Shepherd: Who are a couple of lesser known players Colts fans should get ready to see a lot of this Sunday? Gus Logue: Rookie receiver Josh Cameron has been impressive in limited action thus far this season. Even if Brian Thomas Jr. does not get traded, expect the Jaguars to keep giving Cameron offensive snaps. The Baylor product has been a great glue guy with special teams and run blocking contributions, but he’s also super exciting with the ball in his hands. If you don’t know what folks mean when they say a wideout has “strong hands,” then watch Cameron. Kaevon Merriweather and Rayuan Lane III figure to split snaps at safety in Johnson’s absence, but I would also look for cornerback Montaric “Buster” Brown. He parlayed a career season into a new contract early in the offseason, but a hamstring injury has made him look almost unrecognizable. Jags fans will be praying that he is fully recovered coming out of the bye week. Chris Shepherd: Given a win this weekend Jacksonville will go to 5-2. Do you see a potential for them to make any moves at the trade deadline? What positions might they look to upgrade? Gus Logue: Perhaps they will add depth at offensive tackle after losing Harrison for the season. The more likely scenario is that Jacksonville upgrades its pass defense. The Jaguars have lacked pass rush depth since 2018 (only one year after its historic “Sacksonville” season). For years, the EDGE room has consisted of Josh Hines-Allen, Travon Walker, and a bunch of chumps. And Arik Armstead has been a decent 3-tech but interior push has been lacking for nearly a decade as well. The Jaguars need another pass rusher (Josh Sweat?) to help close out games against elite quarterbacks in January. But I also think that a veteran safety (Jessie Bates?) could fix a lot of communication errors in the secondary, the way Jakobi Meyers stabilized the passing offense last season. Chris Shepherd: The Jaguars are heavy favorites at home this weekend. How do you see this one playing out and what will the final score be? Gus Logue: I see the Jaguars taking care of business and winning by double-digit points. Let’s say 26-13. This is a potential look-ahead spot for Jacksonville, as they will play on Thursday Night Football in Baltimore next week, but they’ll be eager to play at home in new uniforms against a struggling division opponent on Sunday. The Bhayshul Tuten Breakout Game could come this week. And with that, ladies and gentlemen, our week eight preview with the enemy is in the books. I want to thank Gus Logue for giving us some answers to out questions for this week. Here’s to an entertaining and injury free game. As always, go Colts.

title: 3 reasons why the Jaguars beat the Colts
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars didn’t just beat the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday. They absolutely dismantled them. Liam Coen’s team ran out 42-7 winners at EverBank Stadium, producing one of their most complete performances of the season while exposing just how far Indianapolis have fallen. The Jaguars led 28-0 at halftime, added another two touchdowns after the […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 1: Wide receiver Parker Washington #11 of the Jacksonville Jaguars reacts after running for a first down in the second quarter against the Indianapolis Colts at EverBank Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars didn’t just beat the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday. They absolutely dismantled them. Liam Coen’s team ran out 42-7 winners at EverBank Stadium, producing one of their most complete performances of the season while exposing just how far Indianapolis have fallen. The Jaguars led 28-0 at halftime, added another two touchdowns after the break and barely looked troubled throughout. There were plenty of positives for Jacksonville, but there were also some uncomfortable questions for a Colts team that appears to be heading in the wrong direction. Here are three reasons why the Jaguars came out on top. The Jaguars are really good, and the Colts are really bad #Jaguars uniforms today 🐆🐆 pic.twitter.com/JKMxtrwKoc — Jordan Schultz (@Schultz_Report) November 1, 2026 Sometimes, there really isn’t any need to overcomplicate things; Jacksonville is a good football team. Indianapolis, right now, is not. The Jaguars entered this contest with a 4-2 record and an opportunity to strengthen their position in the AFC South. They took full advantage, producing a performance that demonstrated the difference between a team with genuine aspirations and one seemingly searching for answers. There is plenty to like about what Coen is building in Jacksonville. They have an increasingly dangerous offense, a defense capable of making life miserable for opposing quarterbacks and a roster that appears to be developing an identity. Indianapolis, meanwhile, has endured a miserable few weeks. Three consecutive defeats had already raised questions, but the decision to trade away DeForest Buckner and Quenton Nelson suggested the organization was beginning to look toward the future rather than trying to salvage the present. The contrast was stark on Sunday. Jacksonville played with confidence, physicality and purpose. The Colts looked disjointed, lacking in belief and completely outmatched. A 42-7 scoreline might be brutal, but it wasn’t unfair. The better team won, and it wasn’t particularly close. Maybe it was Halloween, maybe it was those COLD rivalries uniforms. But most likely, it was the staggering difference in quality between these two rosters. The Jaguars just dog-walked the Colts. The Jaguars’ defense smelled blood TRICK OR TREAT 🎃 @rayuanlanelll | #INDvsJAX on CBS pic.twitter.com/2zeQtKd5wx — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) November 1, 2026 If there was any hope of Indianapolis making a game of this, Jacksonville’s defense extinguished it pretty quickly. The Colts managed just seven points and endured another difficult afternoon for Daniel Jones. Jacksonville generated pressure, disrupted the Indianapolis running game and capitalized on mistakes whenever they presented themselves. The defining moment came just before halftime. After Trevor Lawrence had fumbled to give Indianapolis an opportunity to get something on the scoreboard, Jones threw an interception that Rayuan Lane III returned 92 yards for a touchdown. Rather than heading into the locker room with some momentum, the Colts found themselves trailing 28-0. It was a devastating sequence for Indianapolis and a perfect illustration of Jacksonville’s defensive approach. The Jaguars weren’t simply waiting for the Colts to make mistakes. They were actively forcing them. Indianapolis finished with two interceptions, and the defense consistently made life uncomfortable for Jones and his supporting cast. There is a growing sense that this Jacksonville defense could be one of the team’s biggest assets as the season progresses. They have playmakers at every level, and when they are playing with this sort of aggression, they are capable of taking games away from opponents. Sunday was a particularly emphatic demonstration. The Jags have weapons all over the field Remember when everyone trashed the #Jaguars for picking Nate Boerkircher in the 2nd round?! Good for him. pic.twitter.com/xfuR2Tzgsv — Jordan Schultz (@Schultz_Report) November 1, 2026 The most encouraging aspect of this victory might have been how many different ways the Jaguars found to hurt Indianapolis. Trevor Lawrence threw three touchdown passes, connecting with Brian Thomas Jr., rookie tight end Nate Boerkircher and Bhayshul Tuten. The latter also demonstrated his explosive potential on the ground, breaking off a 39-yard touchdown run in the second quarter. Chris Rodriguez Jr. added another rushing touchdown after halftime, while Jacksonville finished with a balanced offensive performance. That balance is important. Defenses cannot simply focus on stopping Lawrence and hope the Jaguars struggle to establish their running game. Equally, loading the box to contain the ground attack leaves opportunities for Lawrence to exploit through the air. There are plenty of playmakers for Coen to utilize, and the encouraging thing is that Jacksonville are beginning to find ways to get them involved. Brian Thomas Jr.’s touchdown was particularly welcome given the recent speculation surrounding his future and his inconsistent performances. Getting him back into the end zone could prove significant as the Jaguars look to build momentum. When an offense can hurt opponents in multiple ways, it becomes considerably harder to defend. Jacksonville demonstrated that on Sunday, and there is plenty of reason for optimism if they can maintain that level of production.
