title: Kevin Byard’s first Patriots interception turns the tide against Dolphins
summary: At halftime of the New England Patriots’ rainy road trip to Miami Gardens, FL, trailing the one-win Dolphins 13-3, it had managed only 97 yards of offense. A lost fumble, missed field goal, three-and-out drive and three sacks contributed to a sluggish first half. But the offense, looking dead in the water, rebounded after the […]
full_text: At halftime of the New England Patriots’ rainy road trip to Miami Gardens, FL, trailing the one-win Dolphins 13-3, it had managed only 97 yards of offense. A lost fumble, missed field goal, three-and-out drive and three sacks contributed to a sluggish first half. But the offense, looking dead in the water, rebounded after the intermission, leading to a 24-19 victory . According to head coach Mike Vrabel at the break, New England needed a change in its mentality. That shift materialized when safety Kevin Byard secured a misdirected pass in the fourth quarter, recording his first interception as a Patriot. New England’s offensive woes continued at the start of the second half. A one-yard Drake Maye scramble and a limited three-yard Rhamondre Stevenson rush set the Patriots up for a third-and-six snap. Maye, dropping back to pass, couldn’t find an open receiver, and Dolphins outside linebacker Chop Robinson broke into the pocket and brought the quarterback down for his second sack of the contest. In response, New England’s defense forced Miami into two consecutive three-and-outs. Its offense followed each defensive stop with a touchdown. On the unit’s ensuing series after punting, Maye connected downfield with Kyle Williams for a 43-yard score. Then, the Patriots followed with a 73-yard drive, capped by Maye keeping the ball on a fake pitch-option play and running into the end zone to regain the lead, 17-13. After the Dolphins converted their initial first-down conversion since the opening half, they looked to answer. But five plays into their next drive, signal-caller Malik Willis’ pass deflected off defensive tackle DaQuan Jones’s helmet and traveled 27 yards down the field into the hands of Byard. “[I’m] happy for ‘KB,’” Christian Gonzalez said. “He got his first one of the year. It [generated] good momentum. We talked about it all week. We wanted to come in and break that [turnover] drought, get some picks, get some interceptions, and hopefully take that rolling.” Two plays later, Maye found DeMario Douglas along the right sideline, and the receiver did the rest, carrying the ball 30 yards after the catch and into the end zone for a 48-yard score, extending the Patriots’ advantage to 24-13. “We have to be able to tip passes [and] affect a quarterback,” Vrabel said. “We had the unfortunate [Efton Chism III] fumble there. The defense did a heck of a job in sudden change. So, the more that we can turn the football over, that makes a huge difference, especially on the road, and then the offense to be able to capitalize.” Byard, 33 years old, is a three-time First-Team All-Pro selection who logged a league-leading seven takeaways through the air for the Chicago Bears in 2025. His ball-hawking ability was a key factor in why New England pushed to sign the veteran this past offseason. “It felt excellent. I finally got the monkey off my back to be able to get my first [takeaway] this year,” Byard said. “It was in a big spot, too, because we were able to go up two scores … Hopefully this is just a sign of more to come.” Byard added that the defense has been “preaching” creating turnovers; yet, heading into the contest, the Patriots’ defense has forced just seven in as many games, ranking 20th in the NFL. That point of emphasis stems back to the first few weeks of training camp. With only one turnover through the first six practices of the summer, Byard challenged the safeties to secure more takeaways. Hours later, safety Dell Pettus came away with the defense’s second interception of training camp. Despite allowing a touchdown in the final two minutes of the first half, New England’s defense kept the Patriots within striking distance, allowing the offense to rally and eventually take the lead. At the time of Byard’s takeaway, Miami managed first downs on only two of its eight series. The Patriots’ defensive line also made a significant impact, taking down Willis on five occasions, limiting the Dolphins’ ability to sustain drives.
author: Andrew Guindon

title: 5 winners and losers from Patriots win over the Dolphins
summary: The New England Patriots got back in the win column on Sunday as they topped the Miami Dolphins 24-19. They have now improved to 5-3 on the season. Here is who caught our eye for better or worse upon live-viewing the Week 8 contest. Winners QB Drake Maye: After a slow start in the paint […]
full_text: The New England Patriots got back in the win column on Sunday as they topped the Miami Dolphins 24-19 . They have now improved to 5-3 on the season. Here is who caught our eye for better or worse upon live-viewing the Week 8 contest. Winners QB Drake Maye: After a slow start in the paint conditions while down multiple lineman and top pass catchers, Maye flipped the switch in the second half completing 9-of-10 passes for 146 yards and three total touchdowns. That success came with Maye pushing the ball downfield more, highlighted by a 43-yard touchdown to Kyle Williams on the deep post in a 989 concept. One of Maye’s scores also came with his legs as he kept it himself on a speed option after faking out linebacker Willie Gay Jr. Overall, Maye generated +0.42 EPA per play (90th percentile) as he elevated a banged up unit like the elite quarterback he is. RB Rhamondre Stevenson: Down several skill position players, Stevenson took on a big role offensively with 22 total touches. He took his 19 carries for a game-high 82 yards as the Patriots added some successful wrinkles to get their rushing attack going. Stevenson then iced the game in the fourth quarter recovering an onside kick and converting a first-down on three straight touches. DT Cory Durden: The Patriots defensive line had a strong performance as a whole on Sunday, which was led by Cory Durden. The defensive tackle lived in the backfield for much of the afternoon and ended with 1.5 sacks, three quarterback hits and a pair of run stops. Losers Zone defense: The Patriots entered the week as one of the league’s worst zone coverage defenses in football. Those struggles continued early on Sunday as Malik Willis completed 8-of-10 passes for 93 yards vs. zone in the first-half as the Patriots played 70% of their snaps with eyes on the mobile quarterback. Willis found most of his success on out-breaking routes against off-coverage corners, a game plan the Patriots somewhat got away from in the second-half as they increased their man coverage rate. K Andy Borregales: Back in Miami, Borregales squeaked his first 34-yard field goal in over the right upright before pushing a 40-yard field goal wide right — his third miss from under 50 yards this season. New England’s kickoff coverage also continued to be shaky as they allowed a 36- and 43-yard returns, which Borregales’ tackle saved a potential touchdown. Honorable mentions With TreVeyon Henderson (illness) out, Corey Kiner served as RB2 and broke two runs of 10-plus yards, including a 20-yard gain after an impressive jump cut. It was a solid showing for New England’s limited wide receiver room. Both Kyle Williams and DeMario Douglas found the end zone while Efton Chism paced the group with five catches. Chism’s fumble was the lone blemish. Morgan Moses had some troubles upon live view with the speedy Chop Robinson off the edge while Ben Brown replaced Walter Rouse in the second-half at left guard. Overall, the pressure rate against Maye went down in the second-half. Beyond Durden, Gabe Jacas also tallied 1.5 sacks while Christian Barmore, Elijah Ponder, Jaylen Reed, and Christian Elliss all had 0.5 sacks. The Patriots run defense did a strong job slowing down Ollie Gordon (19 carries, 69 yards) as a whole. Christian Elliss led the charge with four stops. Charles Woods played two snaps and gave up a late 35-yard touchdown as he was beaten off a double move. Kevin Byard recorded his first interception of the season. In the positives on special teams, Mitch Wishnowsky continues to punt well (two i20s) and Marcus Jones had a 26-yard punt return.

title: Patriots playoff picture after win over Dolphins in Week 8
summary: The New England Patriots are 3-0 in the AFC East now. After beating the Buffalo Bills and New York Jets earlier in the year, they have now also taken care of business against the Miami Dolphins. The reigning division champions celebrated a 24-19 victory in the afternoon window on Sunday and have now won five […]
full_text: The New England Patriots are 3-0 in the AFC East now. After beating the Buffalo Bills and New York Jets earlier in the year, they have now also taken care of business against the Miami Dolphins. The reigning division champions celebrated a 24-19 victory in the afternoon window on Sunday and have now won five straight against their rivals going back to last season. What does this mean for the division and playoff standings, however? Let’s find out. AFC East standings Buffalo Bills (6-1) New England Patriots (5-2) New York Jets (2-6) Miami Dolphins (1-6) Playing in the early window of games on Sunday, the Bills secured a 36-10 win over a Ravens team down to its third-string quarterback. Still, they all count the same in the standings, and at 6-1 Buffalo is looking very good in the race for the AFC East crown. The Patriots do hold the head-to-head advantage due to their Week 4 win, but are still trailing by 1.5 games. What can be said with confidence, however, is that the division title will again be decided by those two teams. The Jets losing 38-33 to the Raiders to drop to 2-6 on the year is another sign that they might be headed for yet another rebuild, while the Dolphins couldn’t secure a victory over New England and are therefore still at the bottom of the standings. AFC playoff standings Buffalo Bills (6-1) Denver Broncos (6-2) Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2) Jacksonville Jaguars (5-2) Kansas City Chiefs (5-2) Cincinnati Bengals (5-2) New England Patriots (5-3) On the bubble: 8. Cleveland Browns (5-3) , 9. Las Vegas Raiders (4-4), 10. Baltimore Ravens (4-4), 11. Houston Texans (2- 5) Not yet eliminated, but let’s be real here: 12. New York Jets (2-6), 13. Indianapolis Colts (2-6), 14. Miami Dolphins (1-6), 15. Tennessee Titans (1-7), 16. Los Angeles Chargers (0-7) The playoff picture in the AFC received a major shakeup this weekend, including the Patriots’ position within it. After dropping out of the. top seven seeds last week versus the Chicago Bears, they are now back in courtesy of their 5-1 conference record — a tiebreaker that gives them an advantage over the Browns. The changes go beyond New England moving up a spot. The Bills are the new No. 1 seed due to their win over the Ravens and the Chiefs losing a thriller in Denver. Meanwhile, the Steelers are now atop the AFC North, with Cleveland falling from No. 3 to No. 8. As the battle for playoff positions starts heating up, multiple teams are being left behind. The Jets, Colts, Dolphins, Titans and Chargers all look like they are done already. The Texans are also in danger of their season slipping through their grasps, but they are too talented overall to be counted out just yet.

title: 5 moments that defined the Patriots’ win over the Dolphins
summary: The New England Patriots didn’t play a perfect game against the Miami Dolphins on Sunday afternoon, but their second-half surge allowed them to overcome an early deficit and earn a 24-19 victory on the road. Along the way, they managed to make some impressive plays that put them on the road to victory in the […]
full_text: The New England Patriots didn’t play a perfect game against the Miami Dolphins on Sunday afternoon, but their second-half surge allowed them to overcome an early deficit and earn a 24-19 victory on the road . Along the way, they managed to make some impressive plays that put them on the road to victory in the first place. And so, here is a Patriots-centric view at some of those key moments from the Week 8 contest. Moment No. 1: Continued issues The Patriots entered Week 8 with the second-most giveaways in football, having turned the ball over 14 times in seven games. They added another midway through the first quarter when Efton Chism fumbled the ball while trying to gain some extra yards on a short catch. That's @K_009r with the tackle, @Jacob_R_10 with the punch & @Jbrents_18 with the recovery 👏 📺 @NFLonCBS pic.twitter.com/Dl0dFSfgeM — Miami Dolphins (@MiamiDolphins) November 1, 2026 The play changed the game’s early momentum. While the Patriots appeared to be in control up until that point, Chism’s fumble allowed Miami to get a short field and ultimately tie the game on a 31-yard field goal. It was a play exemplary for New England’s problems in the first half. Moment No. 2: Deep shot Trailing by 10 in the early third quarter, and having gone three-and-out on their first possession of the half, the Patriots were in dire need of a big play. They found it when Drake Maye hit Kyle Williams on a deep crosser for a 43-yard touchdown. TOUCHDOWN, KW 🏈 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/AcObsjWt8v — New England Patriots (@Patriots) November 1, 2026 The play was originally ruled an incompletion after Williams knocked the ball out of his ands with his own knee. However, a review initiated by Mike Vrabel tossing the challenge flag determined that the ball came free after it had already crossed the goal line. And so, the second-year wide receiver’s fifth career touchdown — all of them coming from 30-plus yards out — became official. Moment No. 3: Gutsy call Down three points in the late third quarter, the Patriots had a chance to tie the game at 13-all. However, they decided to forgo a 41-yard Andy Borregales field goal attempt in order to be aggressive: the offense stayed on the field on 4th-and-2 in an attempt to get more out of the Patriots’ next possession after the Williams touchdown than just three points. The plan worked, barely. Drake to Pop to make the FIRST DOWN ‼️ 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/ZBi00RY6Qo — New England Patriots (@Patriots) November 1, 2026 Just like with the Williams touchdown, the replay official had to make the final call on the play. DeMario Douglas was initially ruled short of the line to gain, but the turnover on downs was overruled after a second look. New England maintained possession, and six players later saw Drake Maye waltz into the end after a nifty move to evade a defender from 2 yards out. WHAT A PLAY BY DRAKE MAYE! 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/JsUgKRSAy1 — New England Patriots (@Patriots) November 1, 2026 Moment No. 4: Complementary football After taking the lead on Drake Maye’s touchdown run, the Dolphins suddenly were under pressure again to manufacture some offense. They couldn’t, although Lady Luck was not really on their side either on what turned out to be one of the crucial plays of the day. Byard's FIRST INT as a Patriot 🔥 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/xSTFvJ94wD — New England Patriots (@Patriots) November 1, 2026 A Malik Willis pass attempt ricocheted off of DaQuan Jones’ helmet, and landed in Kevin Byard’s waiting arms. It was the veteran safety’s first interception of the season, and his first in a Patriots uniform after his arrival during the offseason. It furthermore was a big play for a defensive unit that had expressed some unhappiness about the frequency of its takeaways. Moment No. 5: Popping off Just two player after the Byard interception, the Patriots had yet another reason to celebrate. Drake Maye rolled to his right after a fake pitch, left a pass rusher in. his dust, and found DeMario Douglas wide open down the right sideline. The fourth-year wide receiver did the rest. TOUCHDOWN, POP!!! 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/TVjfofNOIu — New England Patriots (@Patriots) November 1, 2026 Douglas caught the pass at the Miami 31-yard line and had a better angle than the first defender, outran a second and juked a third before turning on the jets to reach the end zone. He finished the game with only three receptions, but gained 76 total yards on them and found the end zone once.

title: Instant analysis from Patriots’ win over Dolphins
summary: As the clocks fell behind on Sunday, so did the New England Patriots. But head coach Mike Vrabel’s side went from a 10-point deficit to a 24-19 victory over the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium. Here’s a glance back on the 4:25 p.m. ET kickoff as the 2025 AFC East winners move into November […]
full_text: As the clocks fell behind on Sunday, so did the New England Patriots. But head coach Mike Vrabel’s side went from a 10-point deficit to a 24-19 victory over the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium. Here’s a glance back on the 4:25 p.m. ET kickoff as the 2025 AFC East winners move into November with a 5-3 record. Maye dries off with three touchdowns after halftime Drake Maye accounted for 14 touchdowns during the month of October. The efficiency continued as the calendar turned. The Patriots quarterback completed 16-of-20 throws for 199 yards with two touchdowns and no turnovers in Miami Gardens. He added his third rushing TD of the season to go with a 141.5 passer rating. Beginning in “12” personnel with heavy rain and thunderstorms in the forecast, New England’s eight-play, 35-yard opening drive resulted in a field goal. A fumble by Efton Chism III followed on the second snap of the second series, however, with a punch by linebacker Jacob Rodriguez setting the table for a 3-3 game. And on the third series, a third-down sack by an old friend sent the punt unit on. Down 6-3, Maye evaded pressure and kept his eyes downfield to hit the wide receiver who had fumbled before. But that fourth-and-4 conversion didn’t give way to a tie game. The deficit extended to 13-3 instead. By halftime at Hard Rock Stadium, Maye stood 7-of-10 passing with just 53 scoreless yards through the air. Coming out of it, the Patriots went from punting to challenging what became a 43-yard, pinpoint touchdown pass to speedster Kyle Williams. There was no more sleepwalking from that point forward. The gap closed to 13-10 against a young Dolphins defense fresh off its first win of the fall. New England then took the lead on the heels of a fourth-and-2 effort from slot target DeMario Douglas, as a speed option brought Maye into the end zone to wrap up the third quarter at 17-13. The ball soon went back to Douglas, too. As New England’s QB tested the width of the field, so did the Liberty product en route to 48 yards and his fourth touchdown catch of the campaign for a new career high. Maye did not have pass hit the grass in the second half until 4:20 remained in regulation as three straight drives hit paydirt. Offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels’ group finished 6-of-14 on third down, 2-of-2 on fourth down and 1-of-2 in the red zone. Down No. 1, Patriots’ motley crew of receivers catch all nine targets The Patriots downgraded A.J. Brown to out on the eve of the divisional meeting after the June trade acquisition consecutive practices with a knee issue as well as the high ankle sprain that previously sent him to injured reserve in September. In the absence of No. 1, plus fellow veteran targets Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs, the wide receiver room included three members of the 53-man roster and a former Dolphin checking in as a standard elevation. Two receptions were registered by the depth chart in the first half. Only that didn’t hold. A motley crew of Chism, Williams and Douglas combined catch all nine passes sent their direction for 156 yards and two sprints to the end zone. Rounding out the position was Ryan Miller, who entered Sunday ranked fifth on Miami in receiving yards despite being on New England’s practice squad. But attrition persisted on a Sunday that saw rookies Eli Raridon and Tanner Arkin start and false start at tight end. Captain Hunter Henry went to the locker room prior to intermission and ultimately went from questionable to out due a foot injury . Changing of the left guard New England’s offensive line conceded a total of two sacks over the previous two games. That was the case despite Alijah Vera-Tucker landing on injured reserve with a hamstring injury and Ben Brown also missing time with a knee injury. But the latter subbed back in at left guard for the second half of a soggy Sunday. That’s after the starting five began with a trade pickup from the NFL’s 53-man roster deadline along the interior. The combination included Will Campbell at left tackle, Walter Rouse at left guard, Matt Pryor at right guard and Morgan Moses at right tackle. And Jared Wilson, who had a fumbled snap roll to the QB on third down, was in the middle of things at center. Three sacks were let up. Former Patriot Joshua Uche hit home for the first with a simulated pressure and a stunt. Fellow Dolphins edge rusher Chop Robinson added two more going in and out of intermission. The heat subsided. Stevenson’s hard-earned yards close it An illness kept TreVeyon Henderson sidelined for back-to-back practices before going from questionable to out . Even so, the Patriots’ running backs gained ground to the tune of 126 rushing yards in the absence of the No. 38 overall pick in the 2025 NFL draft. Rhamondre Stevenson’s hard running was leaned on as Sunday wore on. The starter turned 19 carries into 82 yards, including a third-and-5 plunge with no timeouts remaining for the Dolphins. He preceded that 24-19 moment by recovering an onside kick as part of the hands team. Corey Kiner rushed for 38 yards over the course of seven handoffs behind him, led by gains of 10 and 20, while 53-man promotion Lan Larison logged his initial NFL carries. Both backups doubled as kickoff returners. Willis picked once by restocked secondary Malik Willis had to go against a defensive backfield nearing full strength. He wouldn’t outlast it. The Dolphins quarterback went 21-of-32 passing for 211 yards with two touchdowns and one interception while calling his own number only once as a rusher. The afternoon kicked off with a pair of three-and-outs and a field goal for Miami. But a drive featuring the offense’s initial four first downs soon made it a 6-3 game in doinking fashion. The final possession going into the break saw it all come together, though, as an 11-play, 60-yard march to the end zone ended in the hands of wide receiver Malik Washington with a boost from unnecessary roughness. Consecutive three-and-outs were endured heading out of halftime. From there, the Dolphins answered back from a turnover and missed field goal with a 35-yard touchdown to wideout Kevin Coleman. Too little, too late. Carlton Davis III returned to the secondary after missing three straight games due to a neck injury, and the eldest statesman at cornerback started across from All-Pro Christian Gonzalez on Sunday. Veteran safety and captain Kevin Byard III intercepted his first pass in a Patriots uniform in the fourth quarter, too. The March arrival in Foxborough led the NFL with seven picks in 2025. New England’s front forges way to five sacks and 3.2 yards per carry Miami’s QB would be taken down for five sacks against New England’s front. All by halftime. Cory Durden recorded the first 1.5 sacks of his career in the first quarter with help from linebacker Christian Elliss. No. 55 overall pick Gabe Jacas tacked on 1.5 with help from Christian Barmore. And sack leader Elijah Ponder and safety Jaylen Reed also swarmed for a split of their own. The Patriots started the divisional matchup with Dre’Mont Jones off the edge and Ponder, a 2025 UDFA out of Cal Poly who now stands with six sacks on the year, off the ball. Defensive tackles in Durden, Barmore and Milton Williams stood between the outside linebackers in the base front. Behind them stood captain Robert Spillane and the team’s omnipresent leading tackler. The Dolphins managed to turn 23 carries into 74 yards. That ground average of 3.2 yards per was buoyed by a long of 16 from running back Ollie Gordon II. Eventful kicking game Special teams coordinator Jeremy Springer’s department made its presence felt early with a tackle on the opening kickoff by Brenden Schooler and then a 26-yard punt return by Marcus Jones. Things didn’t end there. Patriots kicker Andy Borregales recorded a midfield tackle while in South Florida. The former Miami Hurricane also went 1-of-2 on field goals and 3-of-3 on extra points. He converted narrowly from 34 yards away in the first quarter, but missed wide…

full_text: Update 11/1/2026: Hunter Henry unable to finish Dolphins game with foot injury Hunter Henry exited the Patriots’ 24-19 win over the Miami Dolphins in the second quarter, and did not return. He eventually was ruled out for the rest of the contest in the fourth period. Before being shut down for the day, however, the team captain did make some brief appearances on the sidelines. He returned from the locker room before halftime and tested out his foot before leaving again. The same happened in the early third quarter. Original story 11/1/2026: Hunter Henry questionable to return to Dolphins game with foot injury New England Patriots tight end Hunter Henry departed Sunday’s game early with a foot injury. He is questionable to return. Henry appeared to suffer the injury on a four-yard completion in the second quarter. The veteran spent multiple minutes in the blue medical tent before departing to the locker room. Before departing, Henry was the team’s top receiver with three catches for 30 yards. Rookie Eli Raridon then took over as the top tight end, as the Patriots also have Cameron Latu and rookie Tanner Arkin active at the position. The Patriots entered Sunday already down multiple skill players with wide receiver A.J. Brown and running back TreVeyon Henderson out. Henry and Raridon were set for key roles with just four active wide receivers.

title: Good, bad, ugly from Patriots’ win over Dolphins

If Vrabel looks at his team through those specific categorizations, we shall follow his lead. The New England […]
full_text: Ahead of his first training camp as Patriots head coach in 2025, Mike Vrabel explained that he was judging his team’s performances by three distinct categories: the good, the bad, and the s—t that gets you beat. If Vrabel looks at his team through those specific categorizations, we shall follow his lead. The New England Patriots are back in the win column. Taking on the Dolphins in a rainy Miami on Sunday, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel secured a 24-19 victory to improve to 5-3 on the season. It wasn’t a groundbreaking performance, but one that still allowed the team to head back to Foxborough with some momentum on its side. With that said, let’s dive into our breakdown of the good and the not-so-good from the win at Hard Rock Stadium. The good: Halftime adjustments Judged by the game’s first 30 minutes, the Patriots did not look like a team capable of competing for a playoff spot this year. Despite going up against a one-win team, they were outperformed and found themselves trailing by 10 points heading into the half. Coming out of it, however, they showed some much-needed signs of life. The inconsistency that plagued them early on, especially on offense but also in parts on the defensive side of the ball, became a thing of the past — partially due to improved performance, partially due to some apparent tweaks being made. At first glance, inserting Ben Brown at left guard in place of Walter Rouse and being more aggressive with the man coverage calls seemed to factor into the change. Whatever it was, the Patriots showed more urgency and the results looked the part. The offense in particular did a 180 after being stuck in the mud in the first two quarters: it starting pushing the ball downfield in the passing game and finished drives with touchdowns. After going three-and-out to open the second half, the unit fournd the end zone on three straight possessions to start pulling away. Whatever buttons Mike Vrabel and company pushed during the intermission, it worked. The bad: Procedural issues The Patriots looked uncharacteristically sloppy on Sunday, and one number that reflects this is this: six — that’s the number of pre-snap penalties the team had. On offense, rookie tight end Eli Raridon was flagged for a pair of false starts. On defense, Joshua Farmer, Gabe Jacas, Dre’Mont Jones and Cory Durden were all penalized for lining up offsides; Jones’ infraction negated an interception by teammate Christian Elliss. In addition, the Patriots were flagged two more times for a grand total of eight penalties, and a loss of 46 yards. In the grand scheme of things, those issues were a footnote. That’s partially due to the Dolphins not being good enough overall to challenge New England even with the aided penalty yardage. Other clubs, including the Green Bay Packers next Sunday, appear to be better equipped to capitalize on miscues such as these. The s—t that gets you beat: Missed opportunities After the game’s first three drives, the Patriots appeared to be in full control. They forced a pair of three-and-outs defensively to bookmark a field goal drive. Then, however, came the first of their setbacks: wide receiver Efton Chism getting the ball punched out while trying to gain extra yards after a short reception in the flat. The Patriot had spoken all week about Miami’s aggressiveness attacking the ball, and they were able to get it out on this occasion. The play became a turning point in the first half, and did not only set up a game-tying field goal but also let the momentum shift toward the home team. The same is true for other moments, including Andy Borregales missing a 40-yard field goal, or Craig Woodson dropping what should have been an interception in the early third period. The Patriots had their chances to start pulling away sooner than they did, but they kept stumbling and failed to do a proper job extending or finishing drives. They also played a particularly bad defensive series inside the two-minute warning of the second quarter, allowing Malik Willis to carve up the secondary on a touchdown drive to put his team up 13-3. New England did overcome its early-game wobbles, but it didn’t have to be this way.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Patriots vs. Dolphins final score, highlights, game recap for NFL Week 8
summary: The weather was bad, the start was slow, and yet the New England Patriots still managed to celebrate their fifth win of the season on Sunday against the Miami Dolphins. Visiting their division rivals at a rainy Hard Rock Stadium, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel won 24-19. Early on, it did not look […]
full_text: The weather was bad, the start was slow, and yet the New England Patriots still managed to celebrate their fifth win of the season on Sunday against the Miami Dolphins. Visiting their division rivals at a rainy Hard Rock Stadium, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel won 24-19. Early on, it did not look like the Patriots were on a path to victory. Despite entering the game coming out of a mini-bye, they looked sloppy in the first half. The offense was unable to string plays together and had another turnover, while the defense showed some late cracks. The result was New England trailing 13-3 at the half. In the third quarter, however, the flip was switched. Drake Maye started looking like the MVP candidate he is, tossing two long touchdowns and finding the end zone himself on one occasion. With him leading the way and the defense putting the clamps on Miami, the 10-point deficit was quickly turned into an advantage and eventually a victory. The Patriots are now 5-3 on the year, including 3-0 against the AFC East, while the Dolphins dropped to 1-6. Final score: Patriots 24 : 19 Dolphins Sunday, Nov. 1, 4:25 p.m. ET | Hard Rock Stadium (Miami Gardens, FL) | Broadcast information | Game day roster | Inactives | Weather forecast First quarter Despite winning the coin toss, the Dolphins decided to start the game on offense. The plan did not work out: New England forced a quick three-and-out, with Marcus Jones running the ensuing punt back 26 yards to give his offense possession at its own 49. New England’s offense started in good field position, and did manage to take advantage. Following three straight runs, Drake Maye hit Hunter Henry for a 20-yard gain to bring his team on the cusp of the red zone. However, once inside the Miami 20, the series stalled out. Andy Borregales ended it by splitting the uprights from 34 yards out. | Patriots 3 : 0 Dolphins Miami started its next possession with a big return of its own, taking the kickoff after Borregales’ field goal all the way out to the 47-yard line. However, Cory Durden’s second sack in two drives plus Christian Barmore blowing up a third down on another quarterback takedown forced a second straight quick punt. The Patriots’ next drive was a rough one. First, a Tanner Arkin holding penalty backed the team up. Then, two plays later, Efton Chism lost a fumble while trying to gain extra yards after a short reception. The turnover set up the Dolphins with a first down at the New England 19-yard line. Patriots fans, join the game-day huddle! Luckily for their offense, the Patriots defense continued to play excellent football on the next series to force a quick stop. Cory Durden, who was involved in sacks on each of the first two drives, disrupted another play on second down to eventually help hold Miami to a 31-yard field goal. | Patriots 3 : 3 Dolphins Corey Kiner, who entered the game as RB2 with TreVeyon Henderson out, kickstarted New England’s next drive with a 20-yard carry. The big play did move the team into Dolphins territory, but it once again failed to capitalize: the series ended when ex-Patriot Joshua Uche beat left guard Walter Rouse on a stunt to take down Maye for a 10-year loss on 3rd-and-8. After three straight three-and-outs, running back Ollie Gordon picked up Miami’s first first down of the afternoon. He ended the first quarter with another solid run, and Miami at its own 29-yard line. Second quarter The Dolphins continued moving the ball well coming out of the quarter break, including on a 23-yard pass to Malik Washington against a zone coverage structure. However, the defense shored up on its side of the field. Cory Durden was involved in another tackle for loss, with Elijah Ponder and Jaylen Reed teaming up on a sack. Their efforts did not prevent Miami from taking its first lead of the day, though, when Zane Gonzalez made a 52-yard field goal. | Patriots 3 : 6 Dolphins The Patriots’ next drive showed some promise early on. The team still had to convert a 4th-and-2 to keep the series alive, but Drake Maye shrugging off a sack attempt and finding Efton Chism downfield helped solve that problem. However, he couldn’t get enough on a third-down scramble following a bad snap to move the chains. To make matters worse, Andy Borregales sent his subsequent 40-yard field goal attempt wide to the right to keep the score at 6-3 in Miami’s favor. The Patriots had an opportunity to get the ball back quickly inside the two-minute warning of the first half, but they allowed Miami to convert a 3rd-and-8 while Marcus Jones failed to reel in an interception on the very next play. An unnecessary roughness penalty against Christian Elliss then put the Dolphins squarely into field goal range, with an 18-yard pass giving them 1st-and-goal at the New England 7. Two plays later, the home team was in the end zone for the game’s first touchdown. | Patriots 3 : 13 Dolphins Third quarter The Patriots modified their offensive line coming out of the half, replacing left guard Walter Rouse with Ben Brown. However, the change up front did not lead to a change of fortunes: New England went three-and-out to open the third quarter, with Drake Maye getting sacked on 3rd-and-6 to end the series. New England nearly got a big play on its next drive. However, despite betting his hands on the football, Craig Woodson was unable to complete an interception that would have given the Patriots the ball in Miami territory. The pass breakup still forced the offense off the field on a three-and-out, but it felt like a missed opportunity nonetheless. Rhamondre Stevenson did the heavy lifting early on during the Patriots’ next possession, but it was Drake Maye and Kyle Williams who capped it off in style. Yes, it did take a Mike Vrabel challenge flag to overturn a bad incompletion call on the field, but the end result was a touchdown nonetheless: Maye and the second-year wideout connected from 43-yard out to bring New England within three points. | Patriots 10 : 13 Dolphins TOUCHDOWN, KW 🏈 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/AcObsjWt8v — New England Patriots (@Patriots) November 1, 2026 Miami started yet another drive with a long kickoff return, setting up shop at its own 35-yard line on its next possession. However, an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty against running back Ollie Gordon forced the team into a 3rd-and-20 situation it was unable to convert. Three-and-out. The Patriots followed the recipe that worked on the previous drive on their next possession. Rhamondre Stevenson did some hard running to open the drive, with Drake Maye then hitting DeMario Douglas on a 26-yard gain to get New England into field goal range. Once there, the team bypassed a 41-yard field goal attempt to go for it on 4th-and-2. Initially ruled short of the sticks, a review determined that Douglas had indeed crossed the line to keep the drive alive. Six plays later, Maye found the end zone: he faked the pitch on 3rd-and-goal from the 2-yard line to create an opening, capping off a 73-yard scoring drive in style. | Patriots 17 : 13 Dolphins WHAT A PLAY BY DRAKE MAYE! 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/JsUgKRSAy1 — New England Patriots (@Patriots) November 1, 2026 Fouth quarter The Patriots had been lamenting their lack of takeaways lately, but they got one in the early fourth quarter. A Malik Willis pass bounced off the helmet of defensive tackle DaQuan Jones only to land in Kevin Byard’s waiting arms for the interception. The pick gave New England possession at its own 47-yard line. Byard's FIRST INT as a Patriot 🔥 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/xSTFvJ94wD — New England Patriots (@Patriots) November 1, 2026 It did not take long for the Patriots to take advantage of the interception. Just two plays later, Drake Maye stepped out of a sack…

summary: After one week removed from one of their worst rushing performances in franchise history, the New Orleans Saints have moved on from Run Game Coordinator T.J. Paganetti. When the Saints hired Paganetti, it seemed like an excellent move because of his role in building the historic Super Bowl-winning Philadelphia Eagles’ offensive line. That impact was […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - AUGUST 26: A detailed view of the New Orleans Saints helmet on the field during a practice at Yulman Stadium on August 26, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) | Getty Images After one week removed from one of their worst rushing performances in franchise history, the New Orleans Saints have moved on from Run Game Coordinator T.J. Paganetti. The Saints have parted ways with run game coordinator TJ Paganetti, according to sources. Paganetti came from Philadelphia, where he helped architect the run game and was part of developing one of the league’s best offensive lines — Nick Underhill (@nick_underhill) November 2, 2026 When the Saints hired Paganetti, it seemed like an excellent move because of his role in building the historic Super Bowl-winning Philadelphia Eagles’ offensive line. That impact was supposed to carry over to the Saints’ offensive line and running game, but as we know, those expectations fell short. It’s going to be very interesting to see what changes on the field after this move. With all the pieces of the puzzle involved in the run game and the overall offensive line struggles, Paganetti might just be the first domino to fall. Hopefully, moving on from Paganetti can fix at least some of the running issues New Orleans has had this season, and if that happens, we could see the Saints start to turn this disappointing season around.

full_text: Dominic Zvada (34) and Jordan Sout | Getty Images To complete our bye week look at the New York Giants roster, let’s hand out Kudos and Wet Willies, and offer some thoughts on the team’s specialists. title: Survey results: Giants fans want DL help on the trade market
summary: The New York Giants are on a much-needed bye this week, but that isn’t stopping the flow of news. The 2026 trade deadline is approaching quickly and the Giants remain in the conversation despite not playing this week. The 4-2-1 Giants are in control of the NFC East and while they might not be surprised […]
full_text: Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor carries the ball | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants are on a much-needed bye this week, but that isn’t stopping the flow of news. The 2026 trade deadline is approaching quickly and the Giants remain in the conversation despite not playing this week. The 4-2-1 Giants are in control of the NFC East and while they might not be surprised by their success, the rest of the NFL media landscape is coming around to the fact that the Giants are a real factor in the post-season conversation. We’ve already had reporting that the Giants are approaching the trade deadline with an aggressive mentality to seize their opportunity to separate themselves as an NFC contender. In fact, the Giants are considered the 9th most likely team to make the playoffs at +130 ( per Fanduel ). They still trail the Dallas Cowboys (+108), but have closed the gap in perception. It’s a remarkable rise from being seen as the second-least likely NFC team to make the playoffs when the season started. John Harbaugh and Joe Schoen each tried to convince the Tennessee Titans to trade All Pro DL Jeffery Simmons, but were ultimately rebuffed. The Giants are also believed to be one of the teams pursuing star running back Jonathan Taylor. This week we asked which position Giants fans would like their team to pursue on the trade market. And while they likely would have approved of a trade for Simmons (if not the price), few fans want the team to go after a running back. Almost as many fans want the team to trade for a defensive tackle as the next three options put together. D.J. Reader has been fantastic for the Giants, returning to form in Dennard Wilson’s defense and has quietly been excellent this year. Shelby Harris has been a solid player next to Reader, and we’ve seen flashes incremental improvement from Darius Alexander as well as flashes from Bobby Jamison-Travis and C.J. Okoye. However, the defensive line could still benefit from more depth and talent. The top options of Simmons and DeForest Buckner are off the board. And while it’s possible that the Giants could pry a surprising player loose somewhere, someone like Colts’ nose tackle Grover Stewart stands out as a potential low-cost addition to the defensive line. It isn’t much of a surprise that almost a quarter of fans would rather the team hold their water than make a move. The Giants were burned badly when they attempted to short-circuit their rebuild process following the unexpected success of the 2022 season. Coaching decisions aside, it’s took a couple years to get back on track for a team that mistakenly believed that it was in “win now” mode. Of course, it’s also been widely reported that Harbaugh has believed since the very beginning that the Giants were better than their 2025 record said they were. One of the reasons why he chose the Giants over the Titans or Dolphins is that he believed they have a roster in place to be competitive in 2026. My personal take is that the 2027 NFL Draft promises to be a deep and talented one at several positions of need for the Giants. I’m in favor of using the trade market to add talent if the opportunity cost is in the Giants’ favor and it doesn’t hamper their ability to build the roster for the future. To me, that means using late picks that are unlikely to ever have much impact, or more premium picks if the return is a player who is young enough to be a multi-year contributor and likely to be more impactful than a player than a drafted player. Fewer than 1 in 10 fans, however, want the team to trade for a running back. That runs at odds with John Harbaugh’s desire to add a star “bellcow” to his backfield. Sinking significant resources into the running back position has been a chancy proposition historically. Highly drafted running backs seldom prove “worth it” to the teams that draft them, and high-cost free agents typically only succeed within the structure of a team that’s ready to maximize their potential. We’ve had solid performances from the Giants’ backfield this year, notably against the Dallas Cowboys, Tennessee Titans, and Houston Texans. And considering the trio of Cam Skattebo, Devin Singletary, and Tyrone Tracy (IR) are capable of being a solid grinding unit, the argument is that the Giants don’t need a Ferrari to go get the groceries. The counter to that is that John Harbaugh wants one. It’s also possible that a back who is better able to maximize runs, create on the margins, and turn good runs into explosive runs will have a greater than expected impact on the offense. The hope is that acquiring Taylor (or a player like him) would have a similar impact on the Giants’ offense as Christian McCaffrey and Kenneth Walker III have had on the San Francisco 49ers and Kansas City Chiefs (respectively). On the flip side, it’s surprising to me (personally) that very few fans are interested in acquiring a wide receiver. There’s a tendency among Giants fans to regard receivers as luxury pieces and generally prefer the team to not invest premium resources in the position. So in that regard, I’m not surprised they aren’t in favor of trading for a receiver. However, the Giants’ non-existent depth at the position is a real concern, and the prospect of a “Malachi Fields, Darnell Mooney, Jalin Hyatt” receiving corps isn’t exactly thrilling. There’s also the fact that while the Giants don’t faced stacked boxes all that often (20.4 percent of runs, 21st in the NFL per NextGenStats), they also don’t face light boxes that often. The Giants have only run against a light box on 30.3 percent of the time, which is 25th in the NFL. My position is that not only would adding a primary receiving weapon help insulate the team against a potentially devasting injury, it would do more to enable the Giants to force opposing defenses into more favorable rushing match-ups. But regardless of what the Giants do at the trade deadline, fans are confident. Giants’ fans have largely been confident in the direction of the team since the season started. And while it’s taken some hits over the course of the year, it’s rebounded and risen with every win. We aren’t quite up to the high after the win over the Dallas Cowboys, but the Giants underdog win over the Texans has a similar feel. So while fan confidence took a definite hit after the loss to the Saints, it bounced right back up. That’s to be expected, because even though the Giants had to go to overtime (again), they soundly outplayed the Texans. It’s tough to see fans being down on their team after a great win, particularly heading into an opportunity to get healthy before two divisional games.

title: Giants GM Joe Schoen explains the Jameis Winston extension
summary: New York Giants quarterback Jameis Winston has gone through many ups and downs throughout the first half of the season. Winston went from being the backup that was thrusted into the starting role, but then was benched in favor of J.J. McCarthy following a poor performance against the New Orleans Saints. Winston has seen it […]
full_text: Jameis Winston | Getty Images New York Giants quarterback Jameis Winston has gone through many ups and downs throughout the first half of the season. Winston went from being the backup that was thrusted into the starting role, but then was benched in favor of J.J. McCarthy following a poor performance against the New Orleans Saints. Winston has seen it all this season, and it’s only been less than two months since he signed a two-year, $13 million contract. Giants general manager Joe Schoen explained the reasoning behind Winston’s extension and defended the backup quarterback. “You’re always going to want a vet that can help the young guys while the coaches are up game planning and the quarterbacks are doing film on their own. Downstairs in the meeting room, to have a vet and just to know how valuable Jameis is to Jaxson and how valuable he will be to J.J. as well,” Schoen said. “To have the veteran presence in the room with the wisdom that Jameis has and can provide and the leadership, the multiplier effect that that will pay for those guys down the road is invaluable. So you’re always going to want a vet in the room anyways. And the way that Jameis had performed and along with the leadership, just the chemistry of that room and for the whole team, it just made sense. I’m glad we have him here.” The backup quarterback role isn’t always about stepping into games and performing when the starter gets hurt. The backup quarterback provides a calming presence to the room and sets the tone. It’s a job Winston has grown in and improved at throughout his career. While the Giants may have wished he would have performed better on the field, they are more than pleased with his overall contributions to the locker room and organization. “When you’re talking about a backup quarterback that also has leadership, that can lead not only that room, but the team. Can he go 2-2 in a four-game stretch? He went 2-1-1. And like I said, he’s led us in games where we’ve had leads in the fourth quarter or at least a tie. So you’re in the game in the fourth quarter with him and with a backup quarterback, that’s what you’re looking at,” Schoen said. Winston may not be the starter anymore, but his stint as the starter will have a large impact on how the Giants finish out the year. He may not have been perfect, but he kept the team afloat when they needed him and he’s doing what he needs to do now to be successful in his role. At the end of the day, that’s a pretty darn good backup quarterback.

title: Jets vs Raiders: No defending Jets defense in latest Jets embarrassing loss
summary: In the New York Jets’ eighth game of the 2026 season, on a gorgeous, warm and sunny day in East Rutherford, New Jersey, the Jets lost to the Las Vegas Raiders, 38 – 33. The game opened with the Jets on offense. They got off to an explosive start. A long completion to Garrett Wilson […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - NOVEMBER 1: Dylan Laube #23 of the Las Vegas Raiders returns a kick off for a touchdown against the New York Jets in the second quarter at MetLife Stadium on November 1, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the New York Jets’ eighth game of the 2026 season, on a gorgeous, warm and sunny day in East Rutherford, New Jersey, the Jets lost to the Las Vegas Raiders, 38 – 33. The game opened with the Jets on offense. They got off to an explosive start. A long completion to Garrett Wilson and two long runs by Braelon Allen got the Jets a first and goal at the Raiders two yard line. From there the Jets bogged down, as they never gained another yard. The Jets settled for a short field goal and an early 3 – 0 lead. The lead didn’t last. The Raiders marched right down the field against a Jets defense providing only token resistance. The drive ended when Kirk Cousins found Brock Bowers in the end zone, inexplicably being covered by Travis Brownlee. That matchup went about as you might expect. Touchdown, Raiders. The Raiders had a 7 – 3 lead midway through the first quarter. The Jets answered by grinding out a long drive before settling for a short field goal. At this point the Jets had scored on their first two drives and still trailed 7 – 6 late in the first quarter. The first quarter ended with the Raiders punting after a three and out and the score still Raiders 7, Jets 6. The Jets proceeded to take the ball down the field, with multiple connections to Adonai Mitchell. The drive ended when Geno Smith found Isaiah Williams in the end zone for a touchdown and a 13 – 7 Jets lead early in the second quarter. The Jets lead lasted about 15 seconds. Dylan Laube returned the ensuing kickoff for a touchdown and just like that the Jets trailed the Raiders, 14 – 13. The lead changed hands again shortly thereafter. The Jets drove right down the field. Braelon Allen had a big run and Geno Smith eventually found Adonai Mitchell in the end zone for a touchdown and a 20 – 14 Jets lead midway through the second quarter. Thus far neither defense looked like they had any intention of providing a challenge for the opposing offense. The Jets defense stopped the Raiders on fourth down and the Jets offense took over for what they hoped would be the final drive of the first half. Braelon Allen ran the ball down the Raiders’ throats. Then a miracle happened. With just a few seconds left in the first half the Jets kicked a short field goal. A rare Jets score in the final two minutes of the half closed out the first half scoring. The Jets went into the locker room leading the Raiders 23 – 14, having scored on every drive of the half. The Jets opened the third quarter on defense. It did not go well. The Raiders went right down the field, mixing runs and passes effectively. Eventually Kirk Cousins found Brock Bowers for his second touchdown of the game as both teams continued to play only token defense. The score was now Jets 23, Raiders 21 early in the third quarter. It didn’t take long for the Raiders’ defense to give the touchdown back. After Isaiah Williams returned the kickoff out to the 42 yard line, the Jets moved swiftly down the field. A completion to Garrett Wilson, a completion to Kenyon Sadiq, and a long run by Braelon Allen put the Jets in the end zone. It was the sixth consecutive Jets drive ending in a score. The extra point gave the Jets a 30 – 21 lead midway through the third quarter. It was the first time the Jets scored more than 25 points this season. The Raiders came back. Kirk Cousins marched them down the field and eventually ran it in himself for a touchdown. The shootout was on as the score was now Jets 30, Raiders 28 late in the third quarter. A Jets holding penalty followed by a sack of Geno Smith resulted in the first Jets drive all game that did not end in a score. The Jets punted and the Raiders got the ball with a chance to take the lead in the closing minutes of the third quarter. As the quarter ended the Raiders were close to midfield, moving the ball towards what threatened to be a go ahead score. Ashton Jeanty broke off a big catch and run. A few plays later the Raiders were in the end zone with their third straight touchdown on three second half possessions. That gave the Raiders a 35 – 30 lead early in the fourth quarter as the Jets defense continued to come up small. After the two teams traded three and outs the Jets got the ball. The Raiders had them bottled up with a third and forever, but they bailed the Jets out with a defensive holding penalty. With a new lease on life Geno Smith completed a gorgeous bomb to Adonai Mitchell to give the Jets a first down inside the Raiders’ 15 yard line. Unfortunately the Jets drive stalled from there. The Jets had to settle for a short field goal, making the score Raiders 35, Jets 33 with a little more than four minutes left in the game. On the ensuing possession the Raiders used up all but 27 seconds left in the game on a drive ending in a long field goal, giving them a 38 – 33 lead with 27 seconds left and the Jets out of timeouts. The Jets got to the Raiders 35 yard line before Geno Smith was intecepted in the end zone on a last gasp heave, effectively ending the game. Final score: Raiders 38, Jets 33. The loss brought the Jets’ record to 2-6. Another year of playing out the string for the last two months of the season awaits. The Jets go on the road next week to take on the Kansas City Chiefs. It will be shocking if the Jets are competitive in that game.

We could give out a pre-game or pre-blame ball to the quarterback virtually every week, but that would be boring, so we’re not going to do it. We’ll try to identify somebody besides the quarterback for the glory or the ignominy. This approach comes with the obvious drawback that predictions are difficult, especially about the future. We’re destined to get many of these wrong. No matter. We’ll have some laughs along the way. Let’s get to it. They have averaged less than 97 rushing yards per game, good for 24th in the NFL, and they have averaged just 3.8 yards per carry, good for 26th in the NFL. The Jets have done better lately, averaging 113 rushing yards over the last three games. On Sunday the Jets will get guard Dylan Parham back in the lineup for the first time since game 3 of the season. I don’t know who will be running the ball. Breece Hall may or may not suit up for this game. But whoever is running the ball, this is a game the Jets’ offensive line needs to dominate. Clear holes for the running backs consistently. Allow for long, grinding drives. Give Geno Smith time to throw. That’s how the Jets can win this game. Jets offensive line, come on down! title: 10 Eagles things I think I think from the loss to the Commanders
summary: The Eagles certainly put up a performance for the ages on Sunday Night Football. This was a game where the Eagles needed a win to salvage a season that was on the verge of cratering, and they certainly imploded. Philadelphia’s offense barely mustered 10 points against the Washington Commanders in a 27-10 loss, while the […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 01: Tanner McKee #16 of the Philadelphia Eagles reacts to a unnecessary roughness penalty by K'lavon Chaisson #45 of the Washington Commanders during the second quarter at Northwest Stadium on November 01, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Eagles certainly put up a performance for the ages on Sunday Night Football. This was a game where the Eagles needed a win to salvage a season that was on the verge of cratering, and they certainly imploded. Philadelphia’s offense barely mustered 10 points against the Washington Commanders in a 27-10 loss, while the defense allowed 27 unanswered points after the Eagles took a 10-0 lead late in the first quarter. The Eagles weren’t even competitive against a Commanders team that had just 1 win heading into November. That’s how bad this Eagles team is. While the season isn’t at the halfway point yet, this Eagles season is essentially over. There’s little confidence this team is going to make a run in the lowly NFC East, not with how poor they have played during this six-game losing streak (which is the longest by this franchise since 2012). The Eagles have started 2-6 for the first time since 1999, and there are a lot of aspects from this horrendous performance that need to be dissected. Buckle up. There are some hard truths coming regarding this football team. 1) This offensive line has gotten significantly worse under Chris Kuper. Jeff Stoutland might be the best assistant coach in franchise history. The Eagles were never going to replace him. Unfortunately, the Eagles found an offensive line coach that doesn’t improve his players — at all. Under Kuper, two of the five starting offensive linemen (Landon Dickerson and Tyler Steen) from last season have gotten worse and the two young players (Markel Bell and Drew Kendall) are struggling to improve week in and week out. Bell was abysmal against the Commanders, allowing a 7.0% pressure rate and two sacks while getting dominated by K’Lavon Chaisson all night. Replacing Lane Johnson in a rookie season is a tough task, but Bell is not ready to be a starting right tackle in the NFL. That’s on Kuper and how he’s developing a rookie who is learning how to play right tackle for the first time in his football life. Dickerson allowed a sack and a 4.7% pressure rate, and his pressure rate is 7.8% in the three games he played this seaosn. This was a Pro Bowl player under Stoutland and now he’s a replacement level guard. Jordan Mailata’s performance is even diminishing, as he allowed a 7.0% pressure rate against the Commanders in what wa shis worst game of the season. If the Eagles do decide to move on from a coach this month, Kuper should be the first candidate. 2) The Eagles were right about Tanner McKee this summer. McKee lost out to Andy Dalton in the battle for the QB2 job for a reason. There is enough tape in the three games to demonstrate McKee isn’t good enough to be a starting quarterback in the league. Even with the offensive line decimated by injuries and a poor offensive line, McKee is slow in his progressions and has no mobility to get out of trouble. McKee was abysmal against the Commanders, finishing 23-of-34 for 212 yards with 0 TD, 1 INT and a 72.2 passer rating. He also had a lost fumble in the second half, giving McKee two giveaways on the night. The numbers should have been worse, but 46 passing yards where in garbage time in the final minute to Eli Stowers. Since McKee made his first start in Week 6, he’s completed 63.2% of his passes for 638 yards with 2 TD, 2 INT, and a 76.6 passer rating. McKee is 31st out of 32 quarterbacks in yards per attempt (5.6) and 26th in passer rating. The Eagles offense are 32nd in yards per play (4.2) in the three games with McKee as the starting quarterback, 31st in yards per attempt (5.6), and 29th in offensive points per game (15.0). McKee isn’t the answer as a starting quarterback. He may not even be a QB2 at this rate. The Eagles could try Joe Milton, but the offense won’t move the ball with him either. 3) The second half offense still stinks. Another week the Eagles offense struggled in the second half. Before the Eagles hit the garbage time portion of the game (27-10), the offense ran 32 plays for 91 yards with two giveaways, a missed field goal, and zero points — an abysmal 2.8 yards per play. Whether Jalen Hurts or Tanner McKee is the quarterback, this offense doesn’t move the ball. The Eagles average just 4.6 points per game in the second half, which is last in the nFL. The Eagles are also last in yards per play (3.9), yards per game (116.3), and yards per attempt (5.5). They are 29th in yards per carry (3.4), 30th in passer rating (70.4), and 29th in sack rate allowed (10.4%). McKee was 10-of-14 for 58 yards with 0 TD, 1 INT and a 49.1 passer rating in the second half prior to the garbage time possession at the end of the game — 4.1 yards per attempt. He led the Eagles with 16 rushing yards in the second half at that point, as Saquon Barkley and Elijah Mitchell had 11 carries for 29 yards. Simply put, the Eagles aren’t making adjustments. 4) The second half defense is slightly better. This unit is bad too. They just aren’t at the very bottom of the league like the offense is. The Eagles are 30th in the NFL in points per game allowed (14.1) and 31st in yards per game allowed (198.1). They are 29th in yards per play allowed (5.9) and 32nd in rush yards per game allowed (78.1). The pass rush in the second half isn’t good either, as they are 27th in pressure rate (29.9%) and 27th in sack rate (4.6%). The pass defense is 29th in yards per attempt allowed (8.0). Again, they aren’t at the very bottom of the league. The second half defense is just near the bottom. This is a huge reason why the 2026 Eagles lose football games. 5) In conclusion… The Eagles are arguably the worst second half team in all of football, being outscored 113 to 37 in the second half of games this season. That -76 point differential isn’t even the worst in the NFL, as the Baltimore Ravens sit at -87 following their blowout loss to the Buffalo Bills this week (and the Ravens are on their third-string quarterback too). The yardage differential in the second half of games is -655, worst in the league. The next closest team are the Ravens at -629. The time of possession margin is -2.55 (29th), while the points per drive is 0.84 (32nd), and the three-and-out percentage is 50.0% (32nd). The explosive plays aren’t even there, as the 2.9% 20+ yard play percentage is 32nd in the league. Somehow the Eagles get worse in the second half of games. The personnel isn’t there (at least on one side of the ball), but the struggles go much deeper than that. 6) The run defense is making history. Another week the Eagles defense has allowed 100+ rushing yards to an opponent, as the Commanders had 135 rushing yards against a run defense that was supposed to be a strength of this team entering the year. Instead, the run defense is historically bad — and on the wrong side of history. The Eagles have allowed 100+ rushing yards in each of the first eight games of a season for the first time since 1968, and only the second time in the Super Bowl era. That 1968 team was one of the worst in franchise history, as the Eagles started 0-11 and finished 2-12. They weren’t even bad enough to get the No. 1 pick that year, and the fanbase booed Santa Claus that December as a result. The Eagles have allowed 1,055 rushing yards through eight games, third most in the NFL. The 131.9 rushing yards per game is also 30th, and the most by an Eagles team through eight games since 1998 (146.3). That 1998 Eagles team finished 3-13. This Eagles team is staring at a record that bad based on how poor the run defense is. 7) It’s time to protect Saquon Barkley from himself. Barkley deserves plenty of credit for fighting through his hamstring and back injuries and gutting out performances for an offense that needs him to…

title: Eagles vs. Commanders: The good, the bad, and the ugly
summary: In the last six days, the Eagles’ checkout line has quadrupled. Apathy has arrived on November 1st after the Eagles lost their sixth-straight game, stumbling against the previously one-win Washington Commanders, 27-10, at Northwest Stadium on Sunday night. The last time the Eagles lost six-straight games was in 2012, Andy Reid’s last season that ended […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 01: Stefon Diggs #3 of the Washington Commanders scores a touchdown reception against Kenny Moore II #23 of the Philadelphia Eagles during the second quarter at Northwest Stadium on November 01, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the last six days, the Eagles’ checkout line has quadrupled. Apathy has arrived on November 1st after the Eagles lost their sixth-straight game, stumbling against the previously one-win Washington Commanders, 27-10, at Northwest Stadium on Sunday night. The last time the Eagles lost six-straight games was in 2012, Andy Reid’s last season that ended in a 4-12 finish. Right now, the Eagles, who are 2-6, can only wish that they might win four games this season. It’s where teams that give up go. Yes, the Eagles are that bad (but lately can be used as a great sedative) . Here, it said the Eagles season was through after the 25-14 loss to Carolina in Week 6. Many believe that sentiment now. The Eagles are in sole possession of last place in the NFC East at 2-6, behind 2-4-1 Washington, 3-5 Dallas and the 4-2-1 New York Giants. After Rachaad White’s clinching touchdown with 1:52 left to play, chants of “Eagles suck, Eagles suck,” were heard throughout Northwest Stadium. Who could argue? The Eagles played as complete a game as a lowly, lifeless, capitulating team can. They were awful in all three phases: special teams, defense and offense. In the second half, the Eagles averaged an NFL-low 5.3 yards and 111 yards of offense entering the game managed to even sink below that against Washington, getting shutout in the second half and gaining 155 yards, blown up by cosmetic plays in the last minute. Tanner McKee continues to look skittish in the pocket, on the run, in pretty much anything he does. He was sacked five times for minus-35 yards, completed 23 of 34 for 212 yards with an interception. Washington rushed for 135 yards, making the Eagles the only team in the NFL since 1968 to allow 100 or more rushing yards through the first eight games of the season. Because the Eagles cannot stop the run, defensive coordinator Vic Fangio has been forced to reconfigure his defensive structure, bringing the back end closer to the line of scrimmage. Because Fangio has had to rotate up help in the box, the Eagles are sacrificing deeper areas of the field. The Commanders had plays of 14, 18, 20, 21 (2), 30, 33 and 53 yards. It was Washington’s first comeback win this year, rebounding from a 10-0 deficit. The Eagles cannot pick up a blitz. They cannot handle overloads on one side or the other. They are unable to push the ball downfield. They have the second-longest losing streak in the NFL, behind the winless Los Angeles Chargers. What is even more frustrating, to the fanbase at least, is that the team does not seem to care as they sink. It was revealed last week that numerous sources in and around the Eagles told Bleeding Green Nation that they still trusted and believed in head coach Nick Sirianni and Fangio. That Sirianni still had the locker room. They still somehow believed that Sirianni could turn around this disaster, because he proved he could win. But where there was once unbending support for learning-on-the-job offensive coordinator Sean Mannion and offensive line coach Chris Kuper, that was bending. It has changed to doubt as the Eagles kept sinking. Mannion simply seems overwhelmed. Kuper can’t foresee where unblocked pressures could come from. That was last week. Let’s make a very strong—but very correct assumption—Mannion and Kuper will not be here next season. Maybe sooner than that. Maybe. This team once had leaders. They once had Brandon Graham, Lane Johnson, Jason Kelce, Fletcher Cox, Malcolm Jenkins, Jeff Stoutland and Jalen Hurts. The Eagles have no one like that now. There has been a leadership void. Sirianni apparently cannot fill it. Their minus-65 point differential is the most in the NFC and second-most in the NFL. They have lost to Carolina, Dallas and Washington in successive weeks, three teams with a combined 8-13-1 record, by a collective total of 35 points. Saquon Barkley said it best after the game: “We’re not the big, bad Eagles anymore, right?” Right! The New York Giants are next week. This epic collapse could — and most likely will —get worse. There were crumbs of good, a lot of bad and an Everest of ugly in the Eagles’ 27-10 loss to the Washington Commanders. The Good McKee’s 15-yard scramble on the second play of the fourth quarter. It came on a third-and-four play, and it brought the ball to the Washington 40. McKee had the longest run of the game for the Eagles by six yards. Dallas Goedert’s 16-yard reception on a third-and-seven on the Eagles’ second drive of the second half. It was the Eagles’ longest play of the second half at that point. Three plays later, the Eagles coughed up the ball on a McKee fumble. Jalen Carter making an appearance with a third-quarter 12-yard sack on Washington’s first drive. It was Carter’s first sack since the first half of the Jacksonville game. That was his fourth tackle of the game at that point with 6:20 left to play in the third quarter. Moro Ojomo and Jeremiah Trotter Jr.’s play on Washington’s fourth drive. They combined to make four tackles on the Commanders’ seven plays. It seemed it was either Ojomo or Trotter who were willing to make tackles. Saquon Barkley looking like Saquon Barkley in the first quarter. His 24-yard reception on the Eagles’ third drive set up his three-yard touchdown run with 4:27 left in the first quarter for a 10-0 Eagles’ lead. He was playing hurt, constantly stretching between drives. It was typical Barkley, a team leader doing whatever he had to do to win. The Eagles entered the game outscored 40-10 in the first quarter this season. In the first 10:33 on Sunday night, the Eagles already equaled that total. Barkley had 12 yards rushing on five carries, one reception for 24 yards and the game’s only touchdown on a three-yard touchdown. Imagine having back pain in any walk of life, then compound by eight zillion levels of pain playing in an NFL game. Barkley finished with 30 yards on 13 carries. Barkley deserves to be treated better and not used the way he has been when the season is shot. He is too valuable on and off the field to waste his talents on a wasted season. Safety Andrew Makuba’s jolting shot on Chig Okonkwo that knocked away the ball on Washington’s third drive , causing a fumble, recovered by Zack Baun, and giving the ball to the Eagles at the Washington 26. The turnover led to an Eagles’ 10-0 lead. It was the first fumble recovery the Eagles have had this season. Jake Elliott, among the Eagles’ leading tacklers with 6:10 left in the first quarter, booting a 40-yard field goal to give the Eagles a 3-0 lead. Under the deluge of this season’s Eagles’ incompetence, Elliott’s strong season has been overlooked. He is 6-for-7 this season on field goals, his longest 58 yards, and 16-for-16 on extra points. Elliott missed a 41-yarder in the fourth quarter, after making a 36-yarder, which was wiped out by an Eagles’ penalty. Makai Lemon’s 20-yard reception on the first play of their second drive. It was a good comeback after a slow start on the first drive. McKee started under center and found Lemon wide open at the Washington 42. The play-action slightly slowed the Commanders’ defense for McKee to see Lemon open. The Bad Consecutive penalties on Markel Bell and Jordan Mailata that pushed the Eagles back from a fourth-and-four, to a fourth-and-14 and took points off the board after Elliott kicked a 36-yard field goal. The Mailata penalty wiped that out, pushing Elliott back into attempting a 41-yarder, which ponged off the left upright. Where was Jalen Carter in the first half. Nowhere. On 20 snaps, he had no sacks and one pressure against Washington’s Sam Cosmi. Kenny Moore getting caught inside and having to run over and cover Stefon Diggs slide behind on…
