title: Commanders report card: Team grades in NFL Week 8 win Eagles
summary: The Commanders played horrible football in the first quarter of Sunday’s game against the Philadelphia Eagles. They spotted a beat-up and beaten down Eagles squad 10 points with inexcusable mistakes.  To Washington’s credit, they tightened up after that. The defense locked Philly down and the offense started moving the ball well enough to at least […]
full_text: The Commanders played horrible football in the first quarter of Sunday’s game against the Philadelphia Eagles. They spotted a beat-up and beaten down Eagles squad 10 points with inexcusable mistakes. To Washington’s credit, they tightened up after that. The defense locked Philly down and the offense started moving the ball well enough to at least get a steady dose of field goals. Philly on third down : 5-for-15. Good for Washington’s defense. Commanders on third down: 5-for-13. Meh. Washington rattled off 27 unanswered points after a slow start, which is a win no matter how you slice it. That’s why the Commanders ended up with a 27-10 victory – let’s be real honest here, the Eagles suuuuuuck right now – in a game that keeps them in the NFC East race. Let’s grade out this individual performance in this Week 8 Commanders report card: Rushing offense The Commanders reached 135 yards and a touchdown on 26 carries. Every yard counts the same, but 33 of those came in garbage time, when Rachaad White busted loose for an explosive run with the game already put to bed. Take that run away and White averages 2.0 yards per carry. Yuck. Austin Ekeler was the night’s best runner, and Philly seems committed to keeping Jayden Daniels in the pocket. There’s some concern about Jeremy McNichols’ health (again). That ain’t good. Take that White explosive away and they’re under four yards per carry. Sam Cosmi said he loved the commitment to the run. That was key, but it needs to be better. Grade: B-minus Passing offense Daniels started slow. He was 4-for-11 for 26 yards in the first quarter. He was 12-for-18 for 191 yards and a touchdown after that. So, you know, better. Chig Okonkwo responded well after an early fumble, Treylon Burks led the team with 81 yards on just three catches and Antonio Williams had five catches for 54 yards on a team-high seven targets. And, of course, Stefon Diggs had a huge touchdown catch. Let’s also shout out to right guard Sam Cosmi , who was lights out against Jalen Carter and the Eagles defensive front. Grade: First quarter: F Last three quarters: B Rushing defense Let’s be real clear here. Saquon Barkley wasn’t right. The SNF broadcast crew pointed out that he never sat and was constantly trying to get right and go back in. He didn’t have it and averaged 2.3 yards per carries despite having an early touchdown. Part of that is Philly being a mess up front. Part of that is a Commanders defensive line that played well even without Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw . Eagles running backs averaged just 2.7 yards per carry. Sonny Styles was everywhere and Frankie Luvu was solid. The game ball, here, goes to the Commanders defensive line. Grade: A Passing defense Coach speak will tell you good pass defense is a combination of rush and coverage. On Sunday, the pass-rush pulled some serious weight. Blitzes were getting home quite often, but so many one-on-one matchups were won to produce five sacks and eight quarterback hits. Charles Omenihu was on another level Sunday night and Shy Tuttle stepped up big. K’Lavon Chaisson had some costly penalties but was all around the quarterback. Also. Trey Amos had an interception negated by penalty and nearly had another, but he had a deep-shot PBU that might’ve been his best play of the game. He makes the Commanders secondary so much better. That’s also true with Nick Cross on the back end, leading the team in tackles. Grade: A Special teams Luke McCaffrey was a tone setter in the return game, on the opening drive with a 44-yard kick return and with a 27-yard punt return. The Eagles stayed away from him after all that. Both plays were huge in this game. Kicker Drew Stevens missed a field goal attempt but was integral in this one. He converted four field-goal attempts from 56, 39, 25 and 42 yards to close out this victory when too many Commanders drives ended without a touchdown. Tyler Owens had an ill-timed penalty, but that was the only blemish on a special teams unit that provided a real spark. Grade: A-minus Coaching We’ve given Dan Quinn and rookie coordinators David Blough and Daronte Jones the business in this space thus far. It was all justified. These three were bad during a 1-4-1 start. And it wasn’t just Quinn. After a rough first quarter, things got a lot better. Jones’ pressures got home. Quinn kept things together after a brutal beginning. And Daniels credited Blough with getting calls in earlier and allowing him to dissect things at the line of scrimmage. That’s a win. The continued penalties are not. But, despite the bleak nature of this season’s start (and some coaching issues contributing to it), this team is still fighting. Grade: B How would you grade each phase of the Commanders game in a Week 8 win over the Philadelpha Eagles? Let us know in the comments below:

full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 01: Head coach Dan Quinn of the Washington Commanders and Head coach Nick Sirianni of the Philadelphia Eagles shake hands following the Commanders 27-10 win at Northwest Stadium on November 01, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Washington Commanders had a pretty bad start to their Sunday Night Football game at home against the Philadelphia Eagles. They fell behind 10-0, and didn’t look like they’d be able to score, or not commit penalties. They turned things around and scored 27 unanswered points to put the Eagles firmly in the bottom of the NFC East basement. Dan Quinn spoke to reporters after the game, along with players like Jayden Daniels, Antonio Williams, Trey Amos, and more. Quinn famously said he wanted to see 4 quarters of good football, and said they got 3 tonight. The team’s slow start had a lot to do with the pre-snap penalties the team has been trying to fix all season. There has been talk about simplifying the offense, and the penalties lessened as the game went on and Jayden started heating up. Daniels told reporters that their start to the game was BS and he spoke with the team on the sidelines after several early penalties(including one on him) killed drives. He said he noticed the team getting in and out of the huddle faster after that, and it made the offense run smoother. Jayden Daniels and Antonio Williams both paid tribute to Terry McLaurin who just had knee surgery this week. Williams said they wanted to put a smile on his face as he watched at home while recovering. The rookie is getting more snaps with McLaurin out, and he’s ready to step up into a bigger role in this offense. Williams paid respects to Stefon Diggs as well, and called him a leader in the locker room. title: Key takeaways from Washington Commanders win over Philadelphia Eagles
summary: BOX SCORE  The Commanders struggled to start the season, yet a weak NFC East kept them in contention. They had a bye week to get right and fix the execution, penalties and game management issues that had produced a 1-4-1 record. That’s why, as quarterback Jayden Daniels said, Sunday night’s game against the rival NFC […]
full_text: BOX SCORE The Commanders struggled to start the season, yet a weak NFC East kept them in contention. They had a bye week to get right and fix the execution, penalties and game management issues that had produced a 1-4-1 record. That’s why, as quarterback Jayden Daniels said, Sunday night’s game against the rival NFC East held more weight. A loss would essentially shove playoff chances six feet deep. A win would allow them to make a move, with Dallas losing earlier in the day and the Giants not playing. There was extra time to create solutions to all their problems and emerge victorious and ready for a run of positivity. Instead, we got another hard-to-watch start full of yellow flags and ineffective play. Then, just before the first half ended, things picked up. The offense got going and the defense locked in while asserting itself and earning a hard-fought 27-10 victory over the Eagles in a game they simply had to have. Here are some key takeaways after watching Sunday night’s game: Jayden Daniels does just enough Quarterback Jayden Daniels was inefficient to start this game, seeming out of sync with his receivers working through the air. He got better as the game went on, but he didn’t make the massive negative play that allowed the Commanders to keep adding field goals while erasing a two-score deficit and scoring 27 consecutive points. While Daniels wasn’t awesome, he made a few special plays. That includes this unreal explosive to Treylon Burks: Jayden Daniels —> Treylon Burks for 53 yards! pic.twitter.com/mWbuC8ahiJ — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) November 2, 2026 Stefon Diggs came up huge on this touchdown catch, a turning point in this game: Stefon Diggs showed off some ELITE route running on this TD. 🔥 📺 Sunday Night Football: Eagles at Commanders on NBC and Peacock pic.twitter.com/W0Ov7bAgbj — Sunday Night Football on NBC (@SNFonNBC) November 2, 2026 Daniels completed just 16-of-29 passes for 217 yards and that touchdown – his slow start contributed to that – but found a way to get Washington a win. Rachaad White punctuated it with a 33-yard run and a 1-yard TD plunge a few plays later. Rachaad with the exclamation point ❗️ 📺 #PHIvsWAS NBC pic.twitter.com/E0cSXR9rlX — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) November 2, 2026 No Payne? No problem The Commanders defensive line was decimated by injuries to their two best players, with Daron Payne suffering a season-ending foot fracture on Friday and Javon Kinlaw out for Sunday with a knee problem. Despite the fact one of the team’s best position groups absorbed some huge hits, the line’s healthy members came up big in this one. Charles Omenihu got a huge sack in the second half. Charles on the charge 😤 📺 #PHIvsWAS NBC pic.twitter.com/lOCswntwjZ — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) November 2, 2026 Then he recovered a fumble forced by Dorance Armstrong, following a powerful bull rush, that led to Commanders points. Dorance Armstrong forced the Tanner McKee fumble, and Charles Omenihu recovers! pic.twitter.com/zbJ86EPtvK — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) November 2, 2026 Shy Tuttle also had a sack and was a force in the middle while absorbing more playing time with Payne out. The Commanders brought pressure on Eagles quarterback Tanner McKee to great effect, especially in the second half. Blitzes were often getting home and rattling a true pocket quarterback, but it was impressive to see those up front making big plays against the run and pass considering the injuries to key players. Quinn also brought up third-down performance as an x-factor, and Washington was at its best Sunday night on critical downs. The pass rush produced five sacks and the Commanders gave up just 10 points in its best performance of the year. Penalties (remain) a huge problem The Commanders talked a ton about cleaning up penalties during and coming out of the bye week. Washington average 7.6 accepted penalties per game entering Sunday night, with pre-snap penalties a huge issue driving Quinn crazy. Two false start penalties in a row. "Two teams with a combined 3 wins" Mike Tirico — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) November 2, 2026 Somehow, it was worse. The Commanders had seven accepted penalties in the first half alone, with four false starts among them. While a few were questionable – K’Lavon Chaisson’s first (of two) roughing the passer infraction raised an eyebrow – but most were avoidable. The Commanders finished the game with nine accepted penalties for 70 yards, including a pair of back-to-back penalties that stalled offensive drives. The fact this remains an issue seems crazy how deep we are in this season and that it hasn’t gotten fixed. While execution is always paramount, the types of flags being thrown is on coaching. It’s simply unacceptable at this stage. What were your biggest takeaways from this game? Let us know in the comments below:

title: Sizing up wild NFL Week 8: Lamar Jackson's injury, Bucs' win, Cowboys' collapse
summary: Lamar Jackson's return lasted one snap, the Cardinals upset the Cowboys with their QB2 and RB2, and the Buccaneers won by 16 despite 0 passing yards.
full_text:
What looked like a relatively quiet set of Sunday games in NFL Week 8 turned into something much more unexpectedly dramatic and substantial. The day started with a franchise- and season-altering injury, as Lamar Jackson suffered a thumb injury on his first snap of the game against the Bills , turning the most anticipated matchup of the afternoon into a one-sided blowout.

 By the end of the early slate, eight teams had scored 30 or more points, two games had gone to overtime and one team won in a way we haven't seen since the early 1970s. Throw in a dramatic comeback win for the Broncos in the afternoon and Week 8 was truly wild.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Let's break down six events from an unexpectedly wild Sunday afternoon. I have big plays, bad decisions and quarterback benchings to discuss. It seems natural, though, to begin with the scene in Buffalo, where a Bills blowout was overshadowed by the return and immediate departure of a two-time MVP.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Jackson's short return 
 Cardinals beat Cowboys 
 Bucs go 0-for-3 and win 
 Chiefs blow double-digit lead 
 Titans push Bengals to brink 
 Jeanty, Taylor see surprising work 

 
 

 

 Lamar Jackson 's return from injury lasts one snap 
 Baltimore's day started with Jackson making his return from a left ankle injury and ended with emergency quarterback Joe Fagnano fumbling away a snap for the Ravens' third and final turnover of the day. What happened in between could drastically change the present and future outlook of the organization. After missing 3½ games with a high ankle sprain, Jackson injured his thumb on his first snap of the game against the host Bills and did not return.

 ESPN's Adam Schefter reported that Jackson will require thumb surgery and hit injured reserve, with Baltimore coach Jesse Minter unsure whether the injury will end Jackson's season. For good measure, backup Tyler Huntley suffered a toe injury and was unable to return, leaving Fagnano to take the final 38 snaps of the contest. Unsurprisingly, the rookie free agent wasn't able to do much in what would be a 36-10 Bills victory.

 Minter, general manager Eric DeCosta and the Ravens organization now find themselves at both short- and long-term crossroads. Let's start with the 2026 season. Even if we assume Jackson can make it back later in the season, the Ravens are clearly in a compromised situation. At 4-4, they sit in last place in a very competitive AFC North. They've already traded a future second-round pick for Cam Jurgens  in October and attempted to trade two first-round picks  for Maxx Crosby in the offseason before rescinding the deal after Crosby's physical. Trey Hendrickson , their de facto replacement for Crosby, has two sacks in six games.

 

 With just over a week to go before the trade deadline and his top two quarterbacks both out injured, DeCosta can go in one of two directions. If the Ravens think they have a team that can potentially stay afloat and survive in the playoff picture long enough for Jackson to return, DeCosta could try to swing a trade for another option at quarterback. Jacoby Brissett was  just benched in Arizona. Daniel Jones might be next in Indianapolis, where the Colts could save $13.8 million in cash over the next two years by trading away their embattled starter. Baltimore could also re-sign Cooper Rush , who was in the building last year, albeit in a different offensive scheme. None of those options are going to be very exciting to Ravens fans, but there aren't many high-end quarterbacks available in November.

 Does the rest of this team support making some sort of move? It's tough to believe that's the case. The Baltimore defense has put together good halves of football, but it's 20th in points allowed per possession and EPA per defensive snap. Derrick Henry has averaged 3.6 yards per carry with a 41.8% success rate since Week 2. The decision to re-sign Mark Andrews and let Isaiah Likely leave in free agency has looked disastrous, as Likely has excelled with the Giants while Andrews has been unable to generate any sort of explosion and has dropped four passes. Injuries have also created real problems for the Ravens on the interior, necessitating the trade for Jurgens, who hasn't been a major upgrade since returning from  a concussion he suffered with the Eagles.

 The more practical option might be heading in the opposite direction, writing off any chance of making a serious impact in 2026 and hoping that things will be better with a healthier Jackson in 2027. But outside of veterans like Henry and Calais Campbell , who might prefer not being dealt at this point of their careers, the Ravens don't really have many tradable options. DeCosta won't want to move young cornerstone pieces like Zay Flowers and Nate Wiggins , while the likes of Andrews and Marlon Humphrey aren't playing well enough to attract meaningful trade interest at their existing salaries.

 If he does miss the rest of the year, will Jackson even be part of the equation in 2027? As was  discussed this offseason , his future with Baltimore is tenuous. Jackson has a massive $84.8 million cap number in 2027 to go with no-trade and no-tag clauses. While the Ravens can restructure his contract to create cap room, all that would do is spray dead money on their cap in 2028 and 2029, years when Jackson might be part of another organization anyway.

 The two sides weren't able to come to terms on a contract extension before the season, leaving Jackson with more leverage as he gets closer to unrestricted free agency. Missing most of the season with injuries won't exactly put Jackson's best foot forward, but remember that Dak Prescott was able to parlay a 2020 season abbreviated by a serious ankle injury  into a record-setting contract with the Cowboys because the leverage of unrestricted free agency was more powerful and significant than the blow of the injury.

 

 At the same time, if Jackson did decide after the season that he wanted to leave and gave the Ravens a handful of potential landing spots, would DeCosta really be able to negotiate a significant trade haul? Jackson is a two-time MVP and a future Hall of Famer, but when teams had the ability to negotiate with Jackson on the franchise tag  in 2023, offenses with the likes of Desmond Ridder and Kyle Trask as their nominal starters at the time had no meaningful interest. Negotiating off the tag is different from negotiating a trade, but some of the arguments for  why teams didn't pursue Jackson at the time  were myths, too.

 Since then, Jackson has won a second MVP, come close to winning a third and put together the best passing performances of his career. He's also going to be 30 years old in the 2027 offseason and will have missed significant time in four of the past six seasons. I think Jackson is an absolutely incredible player, and what we saw from him before the ankle injury hinted toward a potentially special season in 2026.

 Getting another team to agree, hand Jackson a record-setting contract and send the Ravens the sort of draft pick haul they would want to justify trading Jackson might not be realistic or possible for DeCosta, though. It would be difficult for Baltimore to accept anything less than what the Broncos sent the Seahawks for Russell Wilson , which included two first-round picks, two second-round picks and three players. Losing Jackson for nothing in 2028 would be disastrous, but trading him for something less than market value in 2027 wouldn't be great business, either.

 Even if Jackson is back next year, the guys lining up around the star quarterback will be different. Henry, Humphrey, Andrews and others could be cap casualties. Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle could earn a head coaching job somewhere, even if the offense struggles without Jackson under center. The Ravens were already facing a potential transition in 2027. That transition might have begun unexpectedly early in western New York on Sunday.

title: NFL Week 8: Big takeaways, questions and fantasy spin from Sunday's games
summary: Our NFL Nation reporters react to all the action, answering the biggest questions coming out of each Sunday game. Here's what we learned from Week 8.
full_text:
The Sunday slate for Week 8 of the  2026 NFL season  kicked off with some shocking results in the early window, including two overtime finishes.

 Ravens quarterback  Lamar Jackson  injured his right thumb on his first snap back after missing three games with an ankle injury, allowing the Bills to cruise to an easy win. The Vikings lost their first game of the season, scoring just 15 points against a Lions defense that had allowed 20-plus points five times in 2026. And despite not completing a pass, the Buccaneers shut out the Falcons.

 In the late window Sunday, the Chargers lost in an L.A. showdown versus the Rams. Patriots quarterback Drake Maye  connected on two touchdown passes of 40-plus yards in a win over the Dolphins. And against the Chiefs, the Broncos completed their fourth fourth-quarter comeback of the season. The Commanders ended the night by beating the Eagles on "Sunday Night Football," sending Philadelphia to its sixth straight loss.

 Our NFL Nation reporters react to all the action, answering lingering questions coming out of each game and detailing everything else you need to know. Fantasy football analysts Matt Bowen and Tristan Cockcroft also have fantasy takeaways from each matchup.

 Let's get to it with the biggest lessons from Sunday.

 PHI-WSH |  KC-DEN |  NE-MIA 
 LAC-LAR  |  TEN-CIN | ARI-DAL 
 BAL-BUF |  LV-NYJ |  MIN-DET

 CAR-GB 

 
 

 

 Washington 27, Philadelphia 10 
 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap 

 

 Commanders 
 Can this win ignite a turnaround for Washington? The Commanders needed this win if just to settle a nervous building, knowing they couldn't afford to lose to a wounded Eagles team at home. But if the Commanders beat the Rams at home next week, then they can talk about turnarounds. Washington committed nine penalties, one of which wiped out an interception deep in Philadelphia territory and continued a season-long theme. Quarterback Jayden Daniels wasn't that sharp, but he made big plays and averaged 13.5 yards per completion against a defense that was healthier than it has been. Daniels got his first win since Oct. 5, 2025, and Washington's defense hounded Tanner McKee all night and held Philly to 3.4 yards per play until late completions boosted that average to 3.9. Maybe this win doesn't represent a turnaround, but the Commanders did what was necessary.

 Trend to watch: With Terry McLaurin done for the season, Washington needs other receivers to help more. Sunday night, Treylon Burks , who is taking over for McLaurin at the X spot, caught three passes for 81 yards, including a 53-yarder. Rookie slot receiver Antonio Williams caught a career-best five passes for 54 yards, including a 30-yard grab. Both receivers set up field goals with their long catches. -- John Keim 

 Next game: vs. Rams (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

 
 

 Eagles 
 Will the Eagles be sellers at the Nov. 10 trade deadline? At 2-6, hope for a turnaround is fading fast. Working with a backup quarterback in McKee and a reworked offensive line that is having trouble holding up, the offense doesn't have anything to rely on, especially with running back Saquon Barkley limited and the Eagles' top receivers ailing. And the defense isn't generating a consistent pass rush. General manager Howie Roseman will not be in fire-sale mode, but as he showed already with the Cam Jurgens trade, he won't be afraid to act if it's the right deal. Philadelphia will hold on to its cornerstone players, but those who are not in the long-term plans could be targeted by teams around the league as the Eagles continue to collect picks in the 2027 and '28 drafts.

 Key stat to know: Jake Elliott was 6-of-6 on field goal attempts before clanging one off the left post midway through the fourth quarter. He had a 36-yarder taken off the board because of an illegal formation call on tackle Jordan Mailata -- the second consecutive penalty on the offense that derailed the drive and sealed its fate. Coach Nick Sirianni stressed the details this week. The Eagles fell short in that sequence, and at various points throughout the game, leading to their sixth straight loss. -- Tim McManus 

 Next game: vs. Giants (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

 
 

 Fantasy football takeaway: Commanders rookie wide receiver Antonio Williams scored 10.4 points in the win over the Eagles, catching a season-high five passes (on seven targets) for 54 yards. With Terry McLaurin (knee) out for the season, Williams' role in Washington's passing game will expand, and he has the route skills and coverage awareness to get open for quarterback Jayden Daniels. At this point, Williams fits as a deeper-league WR3, plus he has potential value as a matchup-dependent streamer in shallower formats. -- Bowen 

 

 

 Denver 28, Kansas City 24 
 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap 

 

 Broncos 
 Can the Broncos compete for a playoff spot with this teeth-grinding offense? Apparently, yes. The Broncos numb the game until it's time to pull it out at the end. Yes, a 15-point fourth quarter with a game-saving, goal-line stand led them to an amazing AFC West win, but they still kicked too many field goals and spent too much time in second-and-long (seven of second-and-7 or more in the first half). Earlier this season, quarterback Bo Nix said it was "exhausting" to have so many possessions go "first down, second down, third down." At least on Sunday, the Broncos were exhausted after a win that put them in first place in the division.

 Trend to watch: The Broncos have continued their comeback ways from 2025, recording a plus-25 point differential in fourth quarters this season (fourth most in the NFL). Since the start of last season, the Broncos are 3-3 in games in which they trailed by 11-plus points in the fourth quarter. The rest of the NFL is a combined 11-215-1 in this scenario since start of last season, and no other team has more than one such win, per ESPN Research. -- Jeff Legwold 

 Next game: at Panthers (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

 

 

 
 

 Chiefs 
 Did the Chiefs just surrender control in the AFC West with their collapse? With 13 minutes left, the Chiefs had the ball and an 11-point lead. Following a disastrous sequence, they are no longer first in their division -- and are left with many regrets. Coach Andy Reid was conservative with his playcalling, and quarterback Patrick Mahomes took a sack on a short-yardage play that forced a more difficult field goal for kicker Harrison Butker , who missed his 54-yarder wide right. The Chiefs' defense also allowed quarterback Bo Nix to complete 5 of 6 passing attempts for 84 yards and a touchdown.

 What to make of the QB performance: For three quarters, Mahomes was excellent, tying a career high with three touchdown passes under pressure and looking more confident as the game progressed. But his decision to not throw the ball away on third-and-2 from the Broncos' 30-yard line, losing 6 yards on the sack, was uncharacteristic and a critical reason for the loss. -- Nate Taylor

 Fantasy football takeaway: Though his day got off to a sluggish start, Broncos RB Jonah Coleman exploded for a pair of big, late plays to seal the team's victory and likely a leading role going forward. Coleman's receiving usage was notable (16 routes, five targets, 10.3 FPTS), and he's a must-add in the 48% of leagues in which he's still available. -- Cockcroft

 Patriots 
 Can the Patriots sustain playing this way? The first half was their worst of the season (just 98 yards on offense), and though they exploded in the second half, they might not be as fortunate over the next two weeks against better competition -- home against the Packers and then against the Lions in Munich. The big plays bailed them out, with quarterback Drake Maye -- who was excellent while facing heavy pressure --…

title: Betting buzz: Cardinals lead charge for big underdogs yet again
summary: Arizona is 4-0 ATS as a seven-point underdog and has three outright wins in that role, including Sunday's stunning comeback at Dallas.
full_text:
Everything that happens in sports has additional context when viewed from a sports betting perspective. From season-changing injuries to record-setting moments and so much more, the sports news cycle will constantly and significantly affect the sports betting industry. 

 Our NFL betting buzz file, with contributions from David Purdum, Doug Greenberg and others, aims to provide fans a look at the sports betting stories that are driving the conversation throughout each week of the season.  

 Key links: NFL futures | Awards odds |  Sports betting home  |  DraftKings   

 
 Nov. 1: Cardinals lead charge for big underdogs yet again 
 By Doug Greenberg 

 It has been a banner season for big underdogs in the NFL, as underdogs of seven or more points have won at least one game outright in each of the first eight weeks -- the first time that has happened since 1971, according to ESPN Research. Underdogs of at least seven points are now 20-7-2 against the spread (ATS) with nine straight-up wins.

 Of all the big underdogs, though, one has stood above the rest: the Arizona Cardinals .

 With their dramatic, come-from-behind overtime win against the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday, the Cardinals notched their third outright victory of the season ... all of which have come when they were underdogs of seven or more points.

 

 Arizona is the only team in the league to be 4-0 against the spread when coming in as an underdog of seven or more points and, oddly enough, their three ATS losses have come when they've been smaller underdogs (they have not been dubbed a favorite yet this season). They were responsible for the largest upset of the 2026 NFL season when they defeated the Los Angeles Rams as 13.5-point underdogs in Week 6.

 In general, the big underdogs' winning and covering has been a welcome development for bookmakers: It's a well-known axiom in sports betting that the public tends to back favorites, both on the spread and as featured in moneyline parlays.

 "Bettors still tend to be hesitant to trust big underdogs, which makes those occasional outright upsets especially valuable for the book," Caesars Sportsbook's head of football, Joey Feazel, told ESPN over email. "That has been a welcome change compared to 2024, when it often felt like the public's preferred teams continued to find a way home. Bettors are beginning to show more interest in taking the points with these underdogs, but we have not seen a widespread shift away from favorites on the moneyline just yet."

 Feazel said that "Arizona was comfortably the most important decision in the book's favor" on Sunday, and DraftKings noted that neither team was heavily backed either way.

 This most recent Cardinals win was particularly improbable. Down by 14 in the fourth quarter, Arizona was as long as 28-1 on DraftKings' live moneyline. Feazel said that some Caesars customers grabbed them in the 12-1 range, but not with significant enough money to cause too much of a problem for the sportsbook, while BetMGM called the Cardinals a "small loser" for the book due to live betting.

 Seven-point underdogs trailing by 14 or more points in the fourth quarter are now 5-977 since 2000, according to ESPN Research. The Cardinals are also the first team in the Super Bowl era to have three road wins as at least seven-point underdogs in their first eight games.

 Arizona began the season with the shortest odds to have the fewest regular-season wins (+250) and was tied with the Miami Dolphins with a preseason win total of 3.5, the lowest in the NFL since 2017. Less than halfway through the season, the Cardinals need just one more win to cash that futures ticket for faithful bettors.

 Their first chance to do so will be in Week 9 when they go on the road to face the  Seattle Seahawks  ... as 11.5-point underdogs, per DraftKings lines.

 
 Oct. 23: Sportsbooks, bettors join the National Tight Ends Day frenzy 
 

 By Doug Greenberg 

 In 2018, the Supreme Court struck down the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act, clearing the way for states to legalize sports betting nationwide. That same year marked the beginning of another momentous occasion that has become a stalwart of NFL betting every season.

 On the fourth Sunday in October -- Oct. 25 in 2026 -- the NFL celebrates National Tight Ends Day, a tongue-in-cheek commemoration of football's most underappreciated skill position. Since San Francisco 49ers tight ends Garrett Celek and George Kittle helped bring the honorary day to life eight years ago, it has become a staple of the betting world, with bookmakers taking extra notice and bettors staking extra cash backing players of the position.

 

 "National Tight Ends Day has become a fun day for football fans, and we've seen the excitement around it grow each year," DraftKings director of sports operation Johnny Avello told ESPN via email. "This is a prime example of a way to have fun with the content on our platform."

 The sportsbook noted that it sees more engagement on tight end player props on National Tight Ends Day than in any other week of a given season. On the day last season (Oct. 28), Hard Rock Bet says it saw tight ends account for 25% of all player prop selections compared to 11% the Sunday before and 9% the Sunday after. For touchdown scorer markets, that number jumped to 42% against 16% and 10% on the surrounding Sundays.

 BetMGM specifically points out that its five most-bet players for props by tickets on the day in 2025 were all tight ends: Dallas Goedert , Tyler Warren , Tucker Kraft , Travis Kelce and Kittle.

 Kraft celebrated by putting up a monster stat line of seven catches for 143 yards and two touchdowns in the Green Bay Packers ' Week 8 win over the Pittsburgh Steelers . Caesars Sportsbook head of football Joey Feazel said that "bettors certainly prospered" by backing Kraft and that the book has had to be more aware of bettor activity during this particular Sunday.

 "This week certainly will increase the amount of action on tight ends in all facets of the games, which in turn has the ability to shorten touchdown prices when the amount of action is significantly increased," Feazel said via email. "But at the end of the day it will simply be the implied probability of each TE to score a touchdown."

 Even with all the hype surrounding tight ends for the day, there are only four players with anytime touchdown odds shorter than +200, according to DraftKings odds as of Thursday evening: Brock Bowers (+110), Trey McBride (+130), Sam LaPorta (+170) and Kraft (+175). Those could -- and probably will -- change closer to kickoff as bettors pile on their favorite TEs and take advantage of the many promotions sportsbooks will be running for the occasion.

 Sportsbooks, like Caesars, also plan to offer special markets, such as most tight end receiving yards, tight end touchdown combos and other milestone props. Last year, Hard Rock offered leaguewide touchdown ladders and a tight end to score in every Sunday 1 p.m. ET game (+1750), among other specialties.

 You can find our bets for National Tight Ends Day here .

 By David Purdum 

 The Los Angeles Rams won over the betting public in the offseason and kicked off the regular season as the clear-cut Super Bowl favorites. They haven't lived up to that billing so far, suffering a new low Sunday.

 The Rams lost to the Arizona Cardinals as 13.5-point home favorites in the biggest upset of the season based on point spread. title: How active NFL players continue to redefine all-time sack list
summary: Myles Garrett's torrid pace up the all-time sack list paces active players making their moves among the greats.
full_text:
Last season, defensive end Myles Garrett won his second Defensive Player of the Year award after setting the NFL's single-season record with 23 sacks with the Cleveland Browns . 
 
 This season, he'll continue his climb up the NFL's all-time sack list as a member of the Los Angeles Rams  after a blockbuster trade  in June -- making the Rams favorites to win the Super Bowl, according to DraftKings Sportsbook, heading into the season. 
 
 Garrett entered the season with 125.5 career sacks, which was tied for 20th in NFL history and third among the other six active players --  Von Miller  (No. 9), Cameron Jordan  (No. 17), Calais Campbell  (No. 25), T.J. Watt  (No. 26), Danielle Hunter  (tied for No. 27) and Khalil Mack  (T-29th) -- in the top 30.  
 
 Joining the top 30 soon could be  Aaron Donald ,  who unretired  to join Garrett on the Rams' defensive line. Donald's 111 sacks currently sits two behind 30th.  
 
 As for Garrett, he entered his 10th season in the NFL averaging approximately 14 sacks per season. If he were to replicate that production, he would tie Pro Football Hall of Famer Jason Taylor, who currently sits at No. 7. If Garrett were to have another historic season, he would surpass Michael Strahan (No. 6) and approach career top-five territory. 
 
 
 
 Miller, who signed with the  Dallas Cowboys  in August, can also pass Strahan in his 15th season -- as he sits only three sacks behind him.   
 
 But Garrett's 125.5 career sacks heading into the season was 10.5 more than any other player since his rookie season in 2017, according to ESPN Research. The pass rusher recorded at least 14 sacks in each of the past five seasons, the longest such streak by any player since 1982. 
 
 If Garrett has 18.5 or more sacks this season, he will hold the record for the most over a two-season span since 1982, according to ESPN Research, and his current ascension up the career list ranks as the second-fastest pace among the top five all time behind only Reggie White's.  
 
As we look at how the sack list is redefined this season, we'll highlight milestones across the NFL landscape 
 We will update this file as the active players move up, and we'll add nuggets and milestones throughout the season. 
 

 

 Week 8 update 

 With two players on bye and Garrett out, only two of the five active players that played this week recorded sacks, but they were impactful. 

 Miller recorded his first sack as a Cowboy Sunday, moving him ahead of Terrell Suggs and into a tie with Jason Taylor for seventh.

 Watt added two sacks of his own, moving him ahead of Simeon Rice and Clyde Simmons for 23rd. He now has 7.5 sacks on the season. 

 

 Week 7 update 

 Hunter and Watt were the only ones to record sacks this week, with Hunter jumping back over Campbell in the rankings. 

 

 Week 6 update 

 With Garrett still out, it was another quiet week on the sack front. Of the active leaders, it was the oldest that recorded the lone sack of the week in Campbell. He moved back in front of Hunter. 

 

 Week 5 update 

 Hunter was the only player among the active leaders to record a sack this week, moving him ahead of Campbell to No. 26 all-time. Hunter now has three sacks through five games. 

 

 Week 4 update 

 Watt kicked off things in Week 4 on "Thursday Night Football" in an impactful way. He had one sack, one forced fumble and a fumble recovery to move his total to 4.5 sacks on the season. Other than that, there wasn't much activity with Garrett continuing to be on IR. 

 

 Week 3 update 

 There wasn't much movement on the list this week with only Mack (1) and Hunter (.5) recording sacks. Watt, Campbell, Hunter and Mack (in that order) now make up 25 to 28 on the all-time list. Along with Campbell, the three top active leaders -- Miller, Jordan and Garrett -- have yet to record a sack this season.  

 

 Week 2 update 

 The second week of the season saw little movement near the top of the career list, but Watt's hot start continues, with the defensive end recording 1.5 sacks to now put him at 3.5 through two weeks (No. 2 in the NFL this season) and break a tie with Campbell to move to 25th. 

 Hunter (27th) and Mack (29th) also recorded one sack apiece over the weekend to break ties and move up one spot on the list. 

 Donald (33rd) made his  season debut on "Monday Night Football" against the Giants after taking two years off. He finished with three tackles, one for a loss, but did not record a sack. 

 

 

 Week 1 update 

 Of all the active sack leaders, Watt was the only one to record a sack, finishing the game with two to move to a tie with Campbell for 25th. 

 And while Donald was held out of the Rams' Week 1 game, Garrett will be out for at least the next four after failing to record a tackle in Australia and landing on injured reserve after having to have arthroscopic surgery on his knee.

 After the Rams' opening loss, Garrett said this was " the worst version of myself that I've put out there."

title: Judging overreactions to NFL Week 8: Days numbered for Schottenheimer, Jackson?
summary: Changes coming in Dallas? Have we seen Lamar's final pass for the Ravens? Could the NFC North go four-for-four? Let's overreact to Sunday's games.
full_text:
Week 8 Sunday was one of those when so much weird stuff happened to make you think, "Maybe we shouldn't overreact to any of this."

 Just kidding. Overreacting is what we do! This is why you come here every Sunday night, to overreact ... or be told you're overreacting.

 So if you want to overreact to an impossible Cowboys loss to a backup Cardinals quarterback, or to the Buccaneers winning a game in which they didn't complete a pass , or games in Cincinnati and East Rutherford that featured more than 70 combined points? Well, go right ahead. You've come to the right place. and we're not going to hold back.

 Here's our Week 8 overreactions column, where we look at five potential takeaways from all the action and judge them as legitimate stances or irrational stretches. Plus, we hit a few fantasy football overreactions at the end.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Lamar has thrown last pass as a Raven? 
 Schottenheimer's days numbered in Dallas? 
 All four NFC North teams in playoffs? 
 Bucs again NFC South favorites? 
 Broncos, Chiefs need deadline WR help? 
 Fantasy overreactions 

 
 

 

 Lamar Jackson has played his final game as a Baltimore Raven 
 Let's consider the facts first. Jackson sat out Weeks 5, 6 and 7 because of an ankle injury . The Ravens went 1-2, with losses to division rivals Cleveland and Cincinnati . Jackson returned for Sunday's game in Buffalo but left after one play because of a thumb injury. After the game, Ravens coach Jessie Minter said Jackson would require thumb surgery and would be put on injured reserve , meaning he has to sit out at least the next four games. Asked if the injury could be season-ending, Minter said, "We'll see."

 Jackson has one year left on his contract after this season. The Ravens approached him about an extension this offseason but no extension was completed . The contract includes a clause that prohibits the Ravens from using the franchise or transition tag to keep Jackson from free agency when it expires after the 2027 season.

 

 Verdict: NOT AN OVERREACTION 

 If -- and this is still a big "if" at this point -- this is a season-ending injury, then the Ravens and Jackson will head into a pivotal, potentially cataclysmic offseason. Jackson's projected salary cap number for 2027 is $84.34 million, which means the Ravens probably will want to extend him to knock down that number. But Jackson isn't interested in talking an extension -- as was the case this past offseason -- so the Ravens will have a decision to make. And if they don't feel comfortable heading into the final year of Jackson's deal without an extension in place, we are going to hear legitimate talk of Jackson being traded. Jackson's contract also has a no-trade clause, which means he'd get to decide where he goes.

 Jackson didn't have that no-franchise clause put in there by accident. He did it so he could have some control over where he plays once the contract is over. And if that place doesn't turn out to be Baltimore, and the Ravens come to that conclusion next spring, it is absolutely possible Jackson is playing for a different team in 2027.

 

 I know that's not what Ravens fans want to hear. At literally any time, Jackson and the Ravens could agree to an extension that renders this speculation moot. But unless and until that happens, these are the possibilities for which you need to prepare yourself as a Ravens fan. That's what the facts indicate.

 

 

 Brian Schottenheimer won't finish the season as Cowboys head coach 
 Holy wow, what a terrible loss that was for the Cowboys on Sunday. Dak Prescott 's rushing touchdown put Dallas up 24-10 early in the fourth quarter against a struggling Cardinals team that benched starting quarterback Jacoby Brissett for Gardner Minshew II earlier in the game. The Cowboys' win probability was over 90% for the entire fourth quarter and was 94.5% with 1:09 left in regulation. But Minshew led an eight-play, 80-yard touchdown drive that tied the score at 30-30 with six seconds left and set up  Chad Ryland  for the winning extra point attempt. Astoundingly, Ryland missed to the left, sending the game to overtime.

 Arizona got the ball first and did nothing before punting it to Dallas, which put the Cowboys in position to win with any score. But they also went three-and-out, with Prescott taking a sack on third-and-8. The Cardinals were then able to get into position for a winning 42-yard field goal, which Ryland hit. The Cowboys and Cardinals are now both 3-5. Dallas is two games behind the first-place Giants in the NFC East after yet another game in which its defense couldn't get the stops it needed, and the offense couldn't quite compensate.

 

 Verdict: OVERREACTION 

 Jerry Jones hasn't fired a head coach in-season since 2010, when he replaced Wade Phillips with Jason Garrett at midseason with the team at 1-7. Jones has said multiple times in the 16 years since that he regretted that decision. It's just not a thing we should expect him to do, and he publicly backed his coach postgame .

 

 This is an incredibly disappointing Cowboys team, and the bloom does appear to be off Schottenheimer after his promising first season. It's certainly possible he won't get a third year as Cowboys head coach if this doesn't turn around. But I do believe very strongly that Schottenheimer will get the chance to do it.

 

 

 All four NFC North teams will make the playoffs 
 Sunday was a big day for the remaining members of the 1972 Dolphins, who are the only team in NFL history to ever complete a perfect season and known to celebrate every year when the final undefeated team loses. That happened Sunday in Detroit, where the Lions overcame a brutal, emotional day of injuries to knock off the previously unbeaten Vikings 19-15 . That result moved the Lions to 5-2, one game behind 6-1 Minnesota in the division. The Bears are 5-2 and play at Seattle on "Monday Night Football." The Packers are 5-3 after Thursday night's victory over Carolina.

 This is only the seventh season in which it has been possible for all four teams from the same division to make the playoffs, since they expanded the playoff field to seven teams per conference in 2020. But it has not happened yet, even though the NFC North and AFC North have both had seasons in which all four of their teams finished with winning records.

 

 Verdict: OVERREACTION 

 As much as I'd love to see this happen, and believe it will someday, I don't think this is the year. It was just last season that all four NFC North teams finished with winning records and if this season ended Sunday, the Vikings would be in as division champs and the other three would be the NFC wild-card teams. But soooo much has to happen for all four to make it. Though it seems certain that the NFC East and NFC South are going to send only one team apiece to the postseason, the NFC West is going to be the roadblock to the NFC North's dream scenario.

 

 The 49ers and Seahawks obviously have good chances to make it, and we expect the Rams to be a factor before all is said and done. Whether it's Minnesota's lackluster offense, Green Bay's porous offensive line, Detroit's injury-riddled defense or ... I don't know, whatever could go wrong in Chicago, someone in the NFC North is bound to struggle just enough to slide behind whoever finishes second in the West.

 

 

 The Buccaneers are going to win the NFC South after all 
 Let's promise to talk about Sunday's Falcons-Buccaneers game very quickly, then vow to never discuss it again. In a driving rainstorm, the Bucs intercepted Falcons QB Michael Penix Jr . four times, threw only three passes of their own, completed none of them ( the first time that has happened since 1974 ) and won 16-0 .

 Tampa Bay rushed the ball 56 times for 324 yards. Bucky Irving had 170 and a touchdown on 27 carries. Kenneth Gainwell had 140 yards on 25 carries. Penix (7.1) and Baker Mayfield 's (2.6) QBRs didn't add up to 10, and QBR is on a 0-to-100 scale. To call this…

title: Steelers' multiple dog-themed jabs at Browns headline NFL Week 8 trolls
summary: NFL teams remained petty in Week 8, led by jabs from the Pittsburgh Steelers aimed at the Cleveland Browns.
full_text:
New month, same pettiness around the NFL, especially with divisional matchups. The Pittsburgh Steelers made the most of their opportunity to troll after defeating the Cleveland Browns on Sunday.

 

 Pittsburgh beat its AFC North rivals 27-6 in a strong defensive display. It sacked Cleveland quarterback Deshaun Watson eight times and forced two turnovers. The Steelers also dominated the ground game with 200 total yards: Jaylen Warren had 143 yards, and  Rico Dowdle collected 56 yards.

 With the "Dawg Pound" being a prominent aspect of the Browns' fan base, the Steelers sent a variety of dog-themed trolls. One of them was an image of a car's reverse camera showing a smiling dog. However, Pittsburgh indicated that it would be reversing into the dog and wrote in the caption on X: "ruh roh." Others included dogs wearing Steelers gear. The main image is a reference to a scene from the 2025 film "Sinners" when Stack, played by Michael B. Jordan, reacts excitedly to Sammie playing the guitar. In this case, he's reacting to the Steelers' final score. 

 

 Here are the top trolls from Week 8.

 

 Buffalo Bills 36, Baltimore Ravens 10 
 The Buffalo Bills took down the Baltimore Ravens at home in a commanding victory.

 Buffalo outgained Baltimore 426 to 144 and averaged 5.6 yards per play. The Ravens' offense stagnated because of in-game injuries to quarterbacks Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley . That prompted the Ravens' third-string quarterback Joe Fagnano to step in early in the second quarter.

 Fagnano's cameo didn't result in a win, but led to a clever post from the Bills. A Baltimore staple, Old Bay seasoning spelled out "Bills Win."

 

 
 Las Vegas Raiders 38, New York Jets 33 
 A high-scoring affair resulted in a win for the Las Vegas Raiders , who held on to beat the New York Jets on the road.

 Las Vegas extended its lead to five points with 27 seconds left in the game. The Raiders then picked off Jets quarterback Geno Smith 's pass to clinch the victory, snapping their four-game losing streak.

 The big win prompted a simple troll playing to the Jets' namesake. Instead of being cleared for takeoff, the Raiders wrote in their post that they were cleared for victory.

 

 
 Los Angeles Rams 24, Los Angeles Chargers 9 
 The Rams won the battle of the two NFL teams in Los Angeles.

 They kept the Chargers scoreless in the second half after falling behind 9-3 with 1:55 left in the first half. The Rams picked off two passes from Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert , both of which led to points.

 After the win, the Rams poked fun at the Chargers' namesake. They shared an image of the Rams' mascot "Rampage" claiming a lightning bolt with the caption: "finders keepers."

title: Ranking the top 10 trick plays in Super Bowl history
summary: Which trick plays cemented their legacies in the Super Bowl? We listed 10 that changed momentum or flat-out won championships.
full_text:
The Super Bowl is the biggest stage in American sports. Millions of people tune in to see the final two teams remaining from the NFL playoffs.

 It's the perfect time for a coach to dig into his bag of tricks and give his players a chance to do the unexpected. But it's also a high-risk, high-reward decision. If it goes right, the coach is a genius, but if it doesn't, his decision will be questioned forever.

 

 Dialing up a trick play at just the right time can catch the opponent slipping and lead to a huge momentum shift, such as Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Nick Foles catching a touchdown pass that led to an upset victory over the New England Patriots . It could also put a game out of reach, such as quarterback Phil Simms' flea-flicker pass to Phil McConkey that put the New York Giants two scores ahead of the Denver Broncos .

 Here are the 10 most memorable trick plays in Super Bowl history:

 COUNTDOWN TO SUPER BOWL LXI: ESPN will televise the Super Bowl for the first time in February. We are counting down to the big game with a Super Bowl Top 10 series, featuring rankings on everything from best catches and performances to biggest upsets, that will run every other Sunday leading up to Super Bowl LXI on Feb. 14, 2027. 

 

 

 1. Philly Special 

 When: Super Bowl LII -- Feb. 4, 2018

 Team: Philadelphia Eagles

 Opponent:  New England Patriots

 Situation: The Eagles were leading 15-12 in the second quarter and facing fourth-and-goal at the 1-yard line.

 Philadelphia desperately needed to answer the Patriots' touchdown, which trimmed New England's deficit to 15-12. Eagles coach Doug Pederson went for it rather than kick the field goal. Coming away with anything less than a touchdown going into halftime, leading by three points, would have been a deflating result for the Eagles, considering New England got the ball back to start the third quarter.

 "When you're playing the Patriots and Tom Brady, field goals don't win games," Pederson said after the game.

 Pederson called a timeout to talk things over with quarterback Nick Foles, who uttered the now-famous words, "Do you want Philly, Philly?" Foles was originally lined up in a shotgun formation before walking to the right side of the offensive line, next to tackle Lane Johnson .

 Jason Kelce snapped the ball directly to running back Corey Clement , pitched the ball to tight end Trey Burton as Foles leaked to the back of the end zone. Burton lofted the pass to a wide-open Foles to put the Eagles up 22-12 at halftime. Philadelphia went on to win 41-33 to secure the first Super Bowl victory in team history.

 

 

 2. "Ambush" onside kick 

 When:  Super Bowl XLIV -- Feb. 7, 2010

 Team: New Orleans Saints 

 Opponent: Indianapolis Colts 

 Situation: The Saints were trailing 10-6 at halftime.

 Saints coach Sean Payton wanted to steal a possession from Indianapolis' high-powered offense, which was led by Hall of Fame quarterback Peyton Manning. The play, which was named "Ambush," called for an onside kick even though teams don't typically do so to start the third quarter.

 The Colts never saw it coming.

 Saints rookie punter Thomas Morstead executed the kick perfectly. Chaos ensued as both teams scrambled for the ball after it bounced off the hands of Colts receiver Hank Baskett. Saints safety Chris Reis recovered the football in the pile.

 "All week we had practiced that onside kick," Payton said. "I told those guys at halftime, 'You've got to make me look good here.' It was a good hit by Thomas, and our guys did a good job of showing a normal kickoff coverage look."

 Quarterback Drew Brees and the offense took over at their own 30-yard line and completed a 59-yard touchdown drive that was capped by a 16-yard pass to running back Pierre Thomas. The decision sparked the Saints to outscore Indianapolis 25-7 in the second half and win the game 31-17. It was New Orleans' first Super Bowl win.

 

 

 3. Antwaan Randle El's pass to Hines Ward 
 When: Super Bowl XL -- Feb. 5, 2006

 Team: Pittsburgh Steelers 

 Opponent: Seattle Seahawks 

 Situation: The Steelers were leading 14-10 in the fourth quarter and facing first-and-10 at the Seahawks' 43-yard line.

 With nine minutes left in the game, the Steelers were looking to throw the knockout punch to secure their fifth Super Bowl title. Coach Bill Cowher believed the Steelers could have success on a trick play that the offense worked on during the Friday practice before the game. The Steelers needed to get near midfield, perhaps just past the 50-yard line.

 Such a moment occurred at the perfect time for the Steelers to utilize the passing skills of receiver Antwaan Randle El, who was a dual-threat quarterback in college at Indiana. Randle El's eyes lit up when he heard the play call, too.

 The Steelers tricked the Seahawks by turning a pitch to running back Jerome Bettis into a reverse for Randle El that turned into a deep pass for fellow receiver Hines Ward. The outcome was one of the most memorable plays in Super Bowl history, a perfect connection from Randle El to Ward for a 43-yard touchdown.

 "Instinctively, it just took me back to being a kid on the playground," Ward said in a recent interview with ESPN. "You see me take, like, two or three hops into the end zone. I didn't know what to do, you know? And words can't describe scoring a touchdown in the Super Bowl. And being in Detroit, seeing the sea of black and gold, waving the Terrible Towel, words can't describe that feeling."

 

 

 4. Robert Newhouse to Golden Richards 
 When: Super Bowl XII -- Jan. 15, 1978

 Team: Dallas Cowboys 

 Opponent: Denver Broncos

 Situation: The Cowboys were leading 20-10 in the fourth quarter and facing first-and-10 from the Broncos' 29 yard-line.

 A takeaway by the Cowboys created the perfect opportunity for the offense to have some fun. After a fumble recovery by cornerback Aaron Kyle, the Cowboys started their possession at the Broncos' 29-yard line. The Cowboys' trickery began when quarterback Roger Staubach pitched the ball to the left to fullback Robert Newhouse. The Broncos' linebackers moved forward because the Cowboys had two pulling linemen in front of Newhouse. In perfect timing, Newhouse invited the Broncos toward him before he turned his hips and threw a pass that traveled 35 yards. Just as impressive as Newhouse's pass was receiver Golden Richards' leaping reception at the goal line. Richards outjumped cornerback Steve Foley for the ball and celebrated his highlight by high-fiving a few of his teammates.

 The moment was historic, too, as Newhouse was the first player who wasn't a quarterback to throw a touchdown pass in the Super Bowl.

 

 

 5. Phil Simms' flea-flicker to Phil McConkey 
 When: Super Bowl XXI -- Jan. 25, 1987

 Team: New York Giants

 Opponent: Denver Broncos

 Situation: The Giants were leading 19-10 in the third quarter and facing a second-and-6 from the Broncos' 52.

 Giants coach Bill Parcells had been known as a more conservative coach who didn't take many risks offensively. Parcells was looking to go up by three scores and let his defense close the deal. So he called for a flea-flicker to generate a big play.

 Simms took the snap and tossed the ball to running back Joe Morris, who tossed it right back. Simms looked downfield and saw McConkey running free and hit him for a 44-yard gain. McConkey caught the pass and got flipped as he was tackled at the 1-yard line. Morris powered his way into the end zone on the next play, pushing the Giants' lead to 26-10.

 The Giants went on to win 39-20. Simms was named Super Bowl MVP and became one of the first to use the phrase "I'm going to Disney World!" after winning the big game.

 

 

 6. Deon Figures' recovery 
 When: Super Bowl XXX -- Jan. 28, 1996

 Team: Pittsburgh Steelers

 Opponent: Dallas Cowboys

 Situation: The Steelers were trailing the Cowboys 20-10 in the fourth quarter.

 Even before the Steelers faced the Cowboys, Cowher had already made a bold…

title: How to bet Bears-Seahawks: Game pick and three props to play
summary: Odds and analysis to help you bet the Chicago Bears-Seattle Seahawks game on Monday night.
full_text:
Monday night's game pits one of the game's best offensive coaches (Ben Johnson) against one of its best defensive coaches (Mike Macdonald) in a heavyweight battle. The Bears have recorded 0.14 EPA per play with Caleb Williams on the field this season, ranking among the five most efficient offenses in the league entering Sunday's play. The Seahawks rank third in EPA per play on defense and are top three against both the run and the pass.

 

 Drill down deeper and we see more specific strength-on-strength matchups: the Seahawks, for example, rank second in pass rush win rate; the Bears are fourth in run block win rate.

 And there will be some added intrigue when the Seahawks offense and Bears defense are on the field, after each team just made major acquisitions. The Seahawks acquired Quenton Nelson from the Indianapolis Colts and the Bears dished out two first-round picks to add Jeffery Simmons from the Tennessee Titans . These two former AFC South foes will draw the spotlight when these units square off, and whoever has the better debut could help decide who wins this game.

 

 

 

 Betting outlook 
 

 ESPN's Football Power Index favors the Seahawks by just 1.8 points in this game, a decent bit short of the full three points by which Seattle is favored. I tend to agree, for what I am guessing is the same reason that FPI likes Chicago relative to the spread: offense is more stable than defense. A good offense is simply more likely to have a strong next game than an equivalently good defense is. And if we isolate the Bears offense to just when Williams is on the field, the Bears offense and Seahawks defense do appear roughly equivalent.

 Plus, Sam Darnold has struggled this season and entered Sunday ranked 23rd in QBR. Give me the Bears +3 .

 

 Notable player props, bets 
 

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Caleb Williams 1+ INT (+100) 

 Liz Loza: Williams doesn't have a reputation for throwing a high number of interceptions. If anything, his proclivity to hold onto the ball too long (and take sacks) keeps his INT numbers low. That has borne out this season, as he has tossed just one pick over four contests. That one pick came against the Minnesota Vikings in a monsoon. The Seahawks don't need inclement weather or heavy blitz packages to tally takeaways, though. Instead, Mike Macdonald generates pressure via stunts and disguises. His methods have clearly worked, as Seattle ranks second in the NFL in takeaways with eight. Williams is still learning, and given his desire to push -- particularly on primetime -- increases the odds of at least one ill-timed toss downfield.

 

 

 Kalif Raymond receptions OVER 2.5 (+136) 

 Walder: Raymond's production has really fallen off, and he failed to make a catch last week. But I can't get this number out of my head: 71. That's Raymond's open score entering Week 8, which is tied for fifth-best among wide receivers and tight ends this season. Open score measures a receiver's ability to get open on all routes, regardless of whether they were targeted, and that's a skill I want to bet on.

 

 Byron Murphy II sacks UNDER 0.25 (-242) 

 Walder: I'll be honest, this isn't my favorite bet in the world. Murphy is having a nice season with 3.0 sacks and a 76th percentile pass rush win rate, and Caleb Williams has taken sacks at a high 8.0% rate this season (up substantially from 3.8% last year). But my sacks model -- which I've been betting successfully for years -- likes the under and I trust the numbers. One reason why is that the model is still going to put some stock into Williams' sack rate from last year, particularly because he missed a few games this season (thus his 2026 sample is smaller than that of other players).

title: A child playcaller? The Bears' Ben Johnson was born for this
summary: Johnson was in middle school when he first started diagramming plays, and we have one of the originals.
full_text:
During the quarterback meeting the night before the C hicago Bears hosted the Philadelphia Eagles on Sept. 29, backup QB C ase Keenum probed coach Ben Johnson over a play he wasn't certain would work.

 Keenum, the 38-year-old journeyman who was starting in place of the injured C aleb Williams , was keen on everything about the play from the route to the protection, and particularly how it was designed, but he had reservations.

 "It was a play Ben was very high on, and I loved it too, but I had some questions about it," Keenum said. "I don't want to say he talked me into it [that] night, but he assured me that it would be a good play. And, golly, he called it at the perfect time."

 With a fresh set of downs at Philadelphia's 41-yard line and 5:55 on the clock in the third quarter, the Bears got a different look after the ball was snapped than what they had anticipated.

 That's when Johnson's virtuosity as a play designer appeared.

 The play was designed to allow the primary receiver to change in a matter of seconds based on the coverage. As he took off from the slot, Kalif Raymond realized quickly that he had become the primary, and the ball was coming his way.

 As Eagles defenders vacated the middle of the field to cover three intermediate routes, Keenum fired a pass into an opening over the middle, where he found Raymond wide-open. The catch-and-run opportunity ended with a 41-yard touchdown as the Bears went on to record a 27-7 rout.

 Those real-time adjustments that Johnson builds into his play designs are something players have come to appreciate. It's what separates him as a playcaller. It's what makes this Bears offense so dangerous.

 

 "The cool part about Ben is he doesn't design plays within the box," Raymond said. "He'll design it based off the voids. Because he's not putting that conceptualized box that everybody pulls from on film, he starts creating his own play within the defensive scheme that you're about to go against.

 "So now he's picking at your voids and [the defense has] to adjust in game."

 The way Johnson designs plays for his offense has built the Bears into one of the NFL's most explosive units as Chicago is off to a 5-2 start. It's a reputation he earned around the league with a scheme rooted in unorthodox designs, trick plays and options, which allows everyone -- yes, everyone -- on offense to get involved.

 "One of the coolest things about Ben is that when he installs a play, like, every play is going to work, every play is going to be an explosive, it doesn't matter if it's a short-yardage run, it doesn't matter if it's a 50-yard bomb," Williams said. "When we get out there, we have full faith in each other as a team, from coaches to players. When you have that, when you have a head ball coach like that, it goes a long way throughout the building."

 Johnson's expertise as a play designer didn't begin when he started calling offenses of his own. His journey can be traced back to his very beginnings in football in Asheville, North Carolina, where he honed his ingenuity as a preteen who designed his own plays while still learning the game. From those roots to the biggest stage in the sport, Johnson has kept tinkering like a mad scientist in a lab, aiming to push the limits of his players and his scheme's capabilities.

 "I can't say the words we use in the offensive meeting room because I'll go viral," Raymond said with a laugh. "It's a borderline between he's got a little bit of genius, a little bit of crazy, a little bit of aggressiveness."

 Ben Johnson, the preteen play designer 

 Gail Johnson, a teacher and busy mom of three, found herself inquisitively staring at the scraps of paper scattered across the floor of her sons' bedroom.

 The tiny scribbles etched in pencil were a part of some code Gail had regularly come across as she tidied up around the bunk beds shared by her young sons Ben and Kyle. Letters "E, T" in succession with a row of circles beneath them, each one containing a number. "QB" was labeled "1," "FB" was "2" and "TB" was "3." There was a long arrow pointing from the circle situated furthest to the left that traced upward before it veered slightly to its right.

 Gail encountered these diagrams so often that she didn't think twice about throwing them away as she made beds and tossed clothes in the hamper. Until one day when Ben, a fifth-grader, inquired about their whereabouts.

 From that point, Gail started saving these drawings and asked her son to explain what they meant. These were football plays, Ben told his mother, who would respond by asking what a specific play was designed to do. As Ben detailed the intent behind the collection of numbers, letters, shapes and lines, Gail transcribed.

 Twins Right Rip 138 backside skinny post 

 Gail smiled as she recognized her handwriting that deciphered the code on one particular drawing, many of which are still housed inside a green folder labeled "keep 'ems" in the family's ranch-style home in Asheville.

 

 "I knew then that his mind was working in that direction, that he was trying to be more creative with the plays that he was probably seeing himself run with his friends," Gail said. "He thought there's more out there, and [he] was going to start fiddling around with it."

 In those days, Sundays were spent gathered around the television watching the San Francisco 49ers dominate the 1990s. The Niners were Don Johnson's favorite team. As a former college offensive coordinator and later a high school football coach, he appreciated San Francisco's West Coast offense and thought quarterback Joe Montana was "exceptional" for the way he operated within the scheme.

 So did Ben, who would jump around the living room and try to throw a spiral with a football that barely fit in his hands while emulating his favorite quarterback.

 On game days, Ben would sit next to his father and ask questions about what he saw unfolding on the screen. He wanted to know why a penalty was called and the reason why certain plays worked and others failed. There was a depth to the questions Ben asked at 10 and 11 years old that Don hadn't heard from the high school players he coached.

 Ben's thirst for an understanding of the game he played from his youth through a walk-on career at the University of North Carolina grew as he began to sketch plays of his own. The lefty expanded his scribbles from scraps in pencil to colorful drawings in marker where the details jumped out immediately to his father. A misdirection play. An angled route where the quarterback throws to the split end, resulting in a touchdown. A play being blocked up by seven players -- "which is unusual," Don notes -- as a pass was thrown away from the play-action and resulted in a receiver being wide-open for a 60-yard touchdown.

 "He wanted to impress his dad, I believe, and he did that with some of the things he [drew]," Don Johnson said.

 Ben sought feedback from his father on the plays he designed. He not only wanted to know if they were legal within the rules of the game, but more importantly, whether Don thought they'd work.

 

 "I tried to tell him I thought he did a pretty good job, but it confused me to see some of the things that he wrote down there," Don said. "So I had to talk with him a little bit more about, here's what actually you could probably do, and he listened very closely. He wanted to do the right thing."

 It was like doing homework for Ben, who would sit at the oval wooden table adjacent to the kitchen and let his mind go to work. He took his affinity for designing plays and furthering his knowledge of offensive football as seriously as he did his academics. By the time he finished high school, he had quarterbacked A.C. Reynolds to a state championship and ranked top-five in his class academically.

 His out-of-the-box thinking and progressive view for pushing the limits on offense were honed after he graduated from UNC and rose from a graduate assistant at Boston…

title: Cowboys trust their talent but failed again in 'unacceptable' loss
summary: Despite an embarrassing home loss to Arizona, the Cowboys remain in the NFC East hunt, but they're "tired of learning this lesson."
full_text:
ARLINGTON, Texas -- There is a star on the nameplates atop the lockers of players who have made a Pro Bowl with the Dallas Cowboys . Eleven of them dot the roster on offense, defense and special teams.

 Three more have made the NFL's all-star game while with another team.

 Making a Pro Bowl isn't the same as being an All-Pro, but talent, it seems, is not the biggest issue for the Cowboys, despite their 3-5 record after a shocking  33-30 overtime loss to the Arizona Cardinals at AT&T Stadium on Sunday.

 "Names don't win games," quarterback Dak Prescott said. "Oh, we've got some great men in that locker room, men that do the right thing and try to come out here and give their best each and every game. We're just not getting it done. That starts with me and goes to any and every guy on this team and coaching staff. So, yeah, I mean, it's the NFL. Names change, names evolve. We've got the firepower, we've got the talent. We've got to be a better team and put it all together."

 

 The only thing propping up the Cowboys' playoff chances at the moment is the state of the NFC East, in which the  New York Giants  are in first place at 4-2-1, followed by the Cowboys (3-5), Washington Commanders (2-4-1) and Philadelphia Eagles (2-6). But the Cowboys have not won back-to-back games since Weeks 11-13 last season, and even with three of their next four games coming against teams with losing records, there are no signs to suggest they can get on a roll.

 Four of the Cowboys' final five games come against teams that are either leading their divisions (Giants, Jacksonville Jaguars ) or had recent playoff successes (defending Super Bowl champ Seattle Seahawks , NFC Championship Game participant Los Angeles Rams ).

 "There's still a lot of football left," Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said. "Character of that room is right. A lot of young players. We're going to go back to work. That's what we do. There's a lot of football left."

 At some point, however, the math will no longer math.

 And at some point, the Cowboys need to win successive games to be considered anything close to a playoff threat. They have done that only once since Schottenheimer took over in 2025.

 The Cowboys are chasing losses to the  Tampa Bay Buccaneers , who were 1-4 at the time and started undrafted rookie quarterback  Jalon Daniels , and now the Cardinals, who lost their starting running back ( Jeremiyah Love ) and receiver ( Kendrick Bourne ) and turned to backup quarterback Gardner Minshew II in the third quarter.

 "Unacceptable," said defensive tackle Kenny Clark , one of the three to make a Pro Bowl outside of Dallas. "Can't lose a game like that."

 

 Said linebacker DeMarvion Overshown , "Tired of learning this lesson."

 The Cardinals had 331 yards on offense, including 160 rushing in the second half, against a defense that includes one of the highest-paid defensive tackles, Quinnen Williams , and former Pro Bowlers Clark, Rashan Gary and DaRon Bland .

 The Cowboys' offense floundered for most of the game. Six days after rushing for 204 yards in a win against the Philadelphia Eagles , they had 93, averaging 2.4 yards per carry. Prescott threw for less than 200 yards for the second time in 2026. In the season-opening loss to the Giants, the reason was a lack of chances. The Cowboys had only seven offensive possessions. Sunday was a lack of execution.

 In overtime, the offense, with Pro Bowlers Prescott, Javonte Williams , CeeDee Lamb , George Pickens and Tyler Smith , had a feeble three-and-out.

 "We had a great chance right at the end to win the game and had everybody out there that can win games for us and of course didn't get it done," Cowboys owner and general manager Jerry Jones said.

 At the midway point of the 2018 season, the Cowboys were 3-5, and lost their first game following the trade for wide receiver Amari Cooper . They went on to win seven of their last eight games to finish 10-6 and win the division, and then they won a playoff game.

 Only Prescott remains from that team.

 The core of the 2018 squad was around for the 13-3 finish in 2016, Prescott's rookie season.

 The core of the 2026 roster, despite all of the recognizable names, has experienced 7-10 in 2024, 7-9-1 in 2025 and now a 3-5 start this season.

 Prescott remembers history but knows it means little.

 "At this point, talk is cheap, telling stories is cheap," Prescott said. "We've got to go write our own story. We put ourselves in this position. Thankfully we've got the pen."

full_text:
Everything that happens in the NFL has additional context when viewed from a fantasy football perspective. From position battles to injuries and so much more, the news cycle will constantly affect player values.

 Our fantasy football buzz file, with contributions from our ESPN fantasy writers and our NFL Nation reporters, aims to provide fantasy managers with the intel they need as news breaks around the league.
